1.summary: MARCH IT BACK: The Marching Illini LIVE in Concert
1.description: Since 1868, the Marching Illini has entertained millions of fans with traditional and innovative performances that have made them “The Nation’s Premier College Marching Band.”  The excellence of innovation continues and is very much alive today as the Marching Illini continues its pursuit of the highest levels of musical, visual, and thoroughly entertaining performances at the historic Memorial Stadium. The Marching Illini is a select organization which annually includes many of the university’s finest and most dedicated students.  Members of the Marching Illini represent virtually every college and major on the university’s diverse campus.  This year’s Marching Illini totals 375 members, which include musicians, guard, the Illinettes Dance Team, drum majors, and the undergraduate and graduate staff members. The Marching Illini halftime show is known for many distinct components, including a modified “ILLINI” formation created by A.A. Harding in the 1920s. Before this takes place, the pregame opener is performed with the Illinois state song, “Patriotic Melody,” “God Bless America,” “Battle Hymn of the Republic” and concludes with “America The Beautiful.” The traditional football halftime show performance includes a medley comprised by parts of “Pride of the Illini,” “March of the Illini” and “Hail to the Orange.” The Marching Illini also plays the national anthem, “Illinois Loyalty,” “Oskee-Wow Wow” and “William Tell” during dynamic formation changes. The Marching Illini has played at many prestigious events, including being the first college marching band to perform the St. Patrick’s Day Parade in Dublin Ireland in 1992, an engagement they repeated six more times. They were also the first college marching band to perform at the London Military Tattoo at Wembly Arena in 2001. Learn more about MARCH IT BACK: The Marching Illini LIVE in Concert

2.description: A mansion. A murder. A mystery. Murder and blackmail are on the menu when six mysterious guests assemble at Boddy Manor for a night they’ll never forget! Was it Mrs. Peacock in the study with the knife? Or was it Colonel Mustard in the library with the wrench? Based on the fan-favorite 1985 Paramount Pictures movie and inspired by the classic Hasbro board game, Clue is the ultimate whodunit that will leave you dying of laughter and keep you guessing until the final twist.   NOTE: THIS IS NOT A MUSICAL.   Run Time  - 80 minutes – No Intermission Age Recommendation - Recommended for ages 12+ Disclaimer - Use of smoke, haze and gunshot sound effects   ©2026 Hasbro. All rights reserved.   Learn more about CLUE - LIVE ON STAGE

3.description: A nostalgic night celebrating over 20 years of amazing hits!For suite availability, pricing and additional information, please contact Illinois Premium Seating at PremiumSeating@Illinois.edu. GRAMMY® Award-winning duo Sugarland has announced the Ride or Die Tour, a 26-city U.S. tour celebrating the 20th anniversary of Enjoy the Ride, the landmark album that cemented Jennifer Nettles and Kristian Bush as one of music's most beloved duos. Since the band's inception in 2002, Sugarland has sold nearly 10 million albums. Achieving an astounding seven No. 1 singles and nearly 2 billion streams to date, some of their most iconic songs include PLATINUM-certified “All I Want to Do” and “Stay,” 2X PLATINUM “Stuck Like Glue,” as well as GOLD-certified “Baby Girl,” “It Happens,” “Settlin',” “Something More,” and “Want To.” Their critical and mainstream appeal have been magnified with industry accolades, including five consecutive CMA Awards for Vocal Duo of the Year (2007-2011), five ACM Awards (including Song of the Year and Single of the Year), and GRAMMY® Awards for Best Country Performance by a Duo or Group with Vocals and Best Country Song for “Stay.” In addition to the global superstardom they've reached with Sugarland, both Nettles and Bush have experienced overwhelming success with their solo work. Most recently, Nettles wrote the book, lyrics, and score for the new off-Broadway musical Giulia: The Poison Queen of Palermo, in which she starred as the title character. The show world premiered in Summer 2026 at the Perelman Performing Arts Center (PAC NYC) at the World Trade Center in New York, directed by Tony winner Mary Zimmerman. As part of Sugarland, Bush helped shape hits including “Stay,” “Baby Girl,” “Stuck Like Glue,” and “Life in a Northern Town,” while also co-founding the acclaimed folk-rock duo Billy Pilgrim with Andrew Hyra and leading projects including Dark Water, Cabin Chill, and a successful solo career. 5.description: The Tony® Award-winning Best Musical that took the world by storm is back. THE WIZ returns “home” to stages across America in an all-new tour, direct from Broadway. The Baltimore Sun raves “Powerhouse performances. Stunning choreography. Visionary sets” and the Chicago Sun-Times proclaims THE WIZ is “An eye-popping and high-intensity revival!” This groundbreaking twist on The Wizard of Oz changed the face of Broadway—from its iconic score packed with soul, gospel, rock, and 70s funk to its stirring tale of Dorothy’s journey to find her place in a contemporary world. Everybody rejoice--this dynamite infusion of ballet, jazz, and modern pop brings a whole new groove to easing on down the road! Learn more about THE WIZ

6.description: Meet Jenna, a waitress and expert pie-maker who dreams of a way out of her small town and rocky marriage. Pouring her heart into her pies, she crafts desserts that mirror her topsy-turvy life such as “The Key (Lime) to Happiness Pie” and “Betrayed By My Eggs Pie.” When a baking contest in a nearby county — and a satisfying encounter with someone new — show Jenna a chance at a fresh start, she must find the courage to seize it. Change is on the menu, as long as Jenna can write her own perfectly personal recipe for happiness. Brought to life by a groundbreaking creative team, this hilarious hit Broadway musical features original music and lyrics by Grammy® Award winner Sara Bareilles (\"Brave,\" \"Love Song\"), a book by acclaimed screenwriter Jessie Nelson (I Am Sam), original choreography by Lorin Latarro (Mrs. Doubtfire, Chess) and original direction by Tony Award® winner Diane Paulus (1776, Jagged Little Pill, Pippin). “WAITRESS is a little slice of heaven!” says Entertainment Weekly, and is “sweet, sassy and passionate,” according to New York Magazine. \"It's an empowering musical of the highest order!\" raves the Chicago Tribune. Don't miss this uplifting and hilarious musical celebrating friendship, motherhood, and the magic of a well-made pie. Learn more about Waitress

7.summary: Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour
7.description: Lindsey Stirling brings her spectacular Snow Waltz Tour to State Farm Center this holiday season. The award-winning violinist, dancer and entertainer delivers a one-of-a-kind holiday experience featuring breathtaking choreography, stunning visuals and Lindsey’s genre-defying arrangements of holiday classics and original music. Blending classical violin with electronic, pop and rock influences, Stirling has created a live show unlike anything else — combining virtuosic musicianship with dance, theatrical production and aerial performance. Her annual holiday tour has become a seasonal tradition, bringing the music of her acclaimed Christmas albums Warmer in the Winter and Snow Waltz to life on stage. $1 per ticket goes towards Lindsey’s foundation, The Upside Fund, which focuses on equitable healthcare and medical debt relief, mental health access, and nutrition education and food justice.   Learn more about Lindsey Stirling - The Snow Waltz Tour

8.description: The New York Times calls it “the best musical of this century.” The Washington Post says, “It is the kind of evening that restores your faith in musicals.” And Entertainment Weekly says, “Grade A: the funniest musical of all time.” Jimmy Fallon of The Tonight Show calls it \"Genius. Brilliant. Phenomenal.\" It’s THE BOOK OF MORMON, the nine-time Tony Award® winning Best Musical. This outrageous musical comedy follows the adventures of a mismatched pair of missionaries, sent halfway across the world to spread the Good Word. With standing room only productions in London, on Broadway, and across North America, THE BOOK OF MORMON has truly become an international sensation. Contains explicit language. For more information, visit TheBookOfMormonTour.com. Learn more about The Book of Mormon

9.description: Maizy and Beau are getting hitched, when the corn that protects their small community starts to die. The town needs answers. But who will dare to venture beyond the borders of Cob County?   Including the knockout songs ‘Woman of the World’, ‘Somebody Will’ and ‘Independently Owned’, this Broadway hit about an unlikely hero, an unscrupulous con artist, and a battle for the heart and soil of a small town, is not to be missed. Learn more about Shucked

94.description: Not Mine Only Held.Join the Asian American Cultural Center for an Artist Showcase featuring Kuhu Shukla and her exhibition, Not Mine Only Held. The exhibition explores themes of identity, belonging, memory, and our connections to people, places, and culture. Drawing on Warli art, an ancient visual tradition of the Warli people of Maharashtra, India, Shukla uses its geometric language alongside influences from the Pacific Northwest to explore memory, myth, emotion, imagination, and our relationship with the natural world. Her work also draws on the story of Maa Sati and Shakti, reflecting on female power, gentle defiance, and the tribulations and triumphs of women across generations.Meet the artist, experience her work, and connect with our community at the opening reception.Location: Asian American Cultural Center, 1210 W. Nevada St., Urbana, ILThe exhibition will be on display from September 11 through December 11, 2026. This program is supported in part by the City of Urbana Arts Grant. This event is open to all eligible persons, regardless of race, color, or national origin.

The exhibition explores themes of identity, belonging, memory, and our connections to people, places, and culture. Drawing on Warli art, an ancient visual tradition of the Warli people of Maharashtra, India, Shukla uses its geometric language alongside influences from the Pacific Northwest to explore memory, myth, emotion, imagination, and our relationship with the natural world. 218.summary: \"Rest Lab 10: Path\" Exhibition | Krannert Art Museum
218.description: Rest Lab 10: Path explores movement as a form of reflection and rest. A winding path invites visitors to explore the meditative and therapeutic potential of movement through their own pace and sensory experience. Supported by soft furnishings, sensory tools, and a sound library, the installation encourages multiple ways of navigating through activity and stillness. Rather than moving towards a destination, Rest Lab is a creative, experimental series that invites resting with intention. Each Rest Lab is unique and encourages visitors to experiment with various ways of taking up space in the galleries of Krannert Art Museum or elsewhere on campus. In the museum, Rest Lab has occupied spaces that otherwise would remain empty as they “rest” between exhibitions. Creating spaces that resist the demands for productivity, urgency, and overexertion, Rest Lab invites visitors to slow down. On view through October 3, 2026. Krannert Art Museum is open Tuesday–Friday, 10–5; Saturday, 10–4; and Thursday until 8 pm, when classes are in session. Exhibitions and events are free and open to everyone! Parking nearby is free after 5 pm and on weekends. Curated by Kamila Glowacki, Assistant Curator of Community Engagement and Learning, and Ishita Dharap, Artist and Educator. Krannert Art Museum acknowledges support from the Illinois Arts Council.
218.location: Krannert Art Museum, 500 E. Peabody Dr., Champaign

228.description: Healthy Habits for Happy Rodents: Nutrition & Welfare Essentials We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Dr. Fernanda Wendt from the Federal University of Paraná (UFPR), Brazil. Date: Tuesday, September 22, 2026 Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online Webinar Dr. Wendt is a veterinarian with advanced training in wildlife and zoological medicine and is currently a PhD candidate in Veterinary Sciences at UFPR. 231.summary: Better Together: Combining the Strengths of Rubin, Euclid, and Roman for Time-domain Science and Cosmology
231.description: We have entered an exciting decade for survey science, with space-based surveys such as Euclid and Roman and ground-based surveys such as Rubin Observatory's Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) providing overlapping imaging datasets across the optical and IR. LSST will identify thousands of tidal disruption events (TDEs) and millions of AGN and supernovae – including hundreds of gravitationally lensed supernovae (gLSNe) from which we can measure the Hubble Constant. I will discuss how joint analysis of ground and space-based data via multi-resolution forward modeling methods is enabling us to identify AGN and TDEs from non-nuclear massive black holes, undertake time delay cosmography with populations of gLSNe, and study the environments of supernovae and AGN. I will also briefly discuss our work on understanding accretion disk physics and radio jet formation in state-changing AGN, which are important probes of super-Eddington accretion and the duty cycle of massive black hole growth.

232.description: The Bike Month Planning group is organizing the 19th annual Light the Night, a bike light giveaway event on Tuesday, September 22, 2026, from 4-7 pm at five locations:  1. Alma Mater Plaza (Intersection of Green St & Wright St, Urbana), 2. Hallene Gateway (Intersection of Illinois and Lincoln, Urbana), 3. Intersection of Green and Lincoln, Urbana, 4. SW of Armory Building (Intersection of Fourth and Gregory, Champaign), and 5. Intersection of Pennsylvania and Dorner, Champaign  Over the past several years, we have installed over 800-1,000 bike light sets every year. Lights will be given out from 4 - 7 pm or until supplies last.  Bicycle registration and Shield pick up will be available at all Light the Night locations.  Safety of bicyclists in our campus community is of the highest importance, and as the days grow shorter in the fall and more people are bicycling at night, it is essential to promote safety measures. Illinois Law requires all bicycles to have lights at night, but it does not require that bikes be sold with light sets and many bicycle riders are not aware of the law. This event is meant to improve safety on campus and in the community by providing bike lights to students, faculty, staff, and community members. Attendees are required to bring their bicycles for the free installation. No registration required.  This event is organized in partnership between the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, Champaign-Urbana Mass Transit District (CUMTD), City of Champaign, City of Urbana, Village of Savoy, Champaign County Regional Planning Commission (CCRPC), and C-U Safe Routes to School Project. Volunteers are needed for this event: Volunteer Sign Up

233.summary: Seminar Series - Areg Danagoulian, Associate Professor, MIT
233.description: \"Cosmic Protons as Arms Control Inspectors: Can we detect nuclear weapons in satellites?\" Abstract: In 2022 Russia launched the Kosmos 2553 satellite into low Earth orbit at ~2,000 km altitude. US officials raised concerns that this satellite may be a test platform for a nuclear-armed anti-satellite weapon—a potential violation of the  Outer Space Treaty that has banned nuclear weapons in space since 1967. The problem: the treaty has never had a verification mechanism. This talk presents a new physics-based approach to this critical gap. At Kosmos 2553's orbital altitude, ~GeV protons trapped in Earth's inner Van Allen radiation belt provide a natural, continuously available interrogation source. We exploit proton-induced spallation in a thermonuclear device's high-Z uranium radiation case to generate characteristic neutron signatures. Our conceptual study shows that an inspector satellite, using a 9U-CubeSat-sized directional neutron detector employing plastic scintillators and CVD diamond veto layers, could detect a thermonuclear warhead from kilometers away. This study informs future verification technologies for space treaty compliance. The talk will cover the physics of Van Allen radiation belt environment, the detection concept of operations, and alternative passive and active detection approaches. Bio: Areg Danagoulian is an Associate Professor of Nuclear Science and Engineering at MIT. He did his PhD research in Experimental Nuclear Physics at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. Areg’s PhD thesis focused on experiments that used real Compton scattering on the proton at 2-6GeV, allowing to probe the proton’s internal structure and understand how it couples to external excitations. Afther his PhD Areg worked at Los Alamos as a postdoctoral researcher, and then as a senior scientist at Passport Systems, Inc. (PSI). 252.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 289.summary: GGIS Colloquium | Gabriela Valdivia, \"Where Thought and Place Are One: Yakui Yachana and the Art of Mapping With Amazonian Places\"
289.description: Gabriela Valdivia \"Where Thought and Place Are One: Yakui Yachana and the Art of Mapping With Amazonian Places.\" Valdivia is a professor in the Department of Geography at UNC-Chapel Hill and Assistant Dean at Honors Carolina.  Alli puncha, causanguichu. Are you with life, are you living? This talk shares Yakui Yachana, a multi-year collaborative mapping project with Napo Runa peoples of the Ecuadorian Amazon. Part art exhibit, part storytelling, part method for grounded normativity, we ask what becomes possible when we \"amazonize\" cartography — mapping with, rather than about, Amazonian places. Drawing on participatory workshops with the community of Nuevo Santo Domingo del Río Hollín, we follow hand-drawn maps that hold rivers, forests, and spirits as kin rather than coordinates: maps where vanishing points open onto myth-time, where lines carry ayllu and llacta, or a sense of home, and where being known by a place matters as much as knowing it. We ask not what these drawings show, but where they lead us — and what it might mean to map otherwise, on Amazonian peoples' own termsGabriela is a feminist political ecologist examining the relationship between resources and socio-environmental inequities. Her research and teaching focus on how environmental injustices shape everyday life experiences and decisions in the Americas. She is an author of the digital project Crude Entanglements, which explores the affective dimensions of oil production; a co-author of Oil, Revolution, and Indigenous Citizenship in Ecuadorian Amazonia; and a co-editor of the Routledge Handbook of Critical Resource Geography. She grew up in Peru and conducted ethnographic research in Ecuador and Bolivia, and brings these experiences into her courses on Latin American environments and societies and advanced undergraduate courses on political ecology and global environmental justice.  Learn more about Gabriela by visiting her website: https://valdivia.web.unc.edu/.

Volunteers gather at the Literatures, Cultures and Linguistics Buildling at 5 p.m. for brief instructions, then form lights-out brigades that fan out across campus to shut off lights for the weekend! Volunteering takes about an hour and a half — and you can get a cookie for your efforts! Join us to help save energy, cut utility costs, and avert emissions!NOTE: You must register separately for each ILO date. Please sign up individually even if you are part of an RSO so we can plan for enough treats! For more information, visit: https://isee.illinois.edu/campus-sustainability/get-involved/ilo/
291.location: Literatures, Cultures and Linguistics Building, 707 S. Mathews Ave., Urbana

295.description: Tsukimi (月見) or O-tsukimi (お月見) is a holiday that celebrates the beauty of the Harvest Moon. Influenced by the Chinese Mid-Autumn Festival, this special night has become a unique Japanese custom of holding moon-viewing parties featuring special food and beautiful decorations for thousands of years. Note: Japan House will NOT be open to the public during Tsukimi and there are no public restrooms in the Arboretum. All activities will take place outside so please plan accordingly. The matcha cafe will be open at 6:30pm. Each year at Japan House, we offer the opportunity for guests to view a tea ceremony and to celebrate the full moon together in the beauty of the gardens. At 6pm, floral artist and Ikenobo ikebana teacher Reiko Takahashi will be making a special ikebana arrangement called \"tatehana\" as an offering to the Moon. Professor Emeritus Kimiko Gunji will perform a special tea ceremony in the Japan House Gardens to honor the Harvest Moon for all to watch. Japan House interns will be floating lanterns to illuminate the ponds and guests are welcome to stroll through the area for this solemn occasion. In the south driveway, Japan House will have a pop-up matcha cafe offering joyo manju and iced sencha (green tea) for sale at 6:30pm. Pre-orders are welcome online and limited quantities are available for walk-up purchases. The cafe will open once the tea ceremony is complete and an offering is made to the moon. The joyo manju is gluten-free, nut-free, and vegan! Sponsor a floating lantern! Guests are welcome to make a donation and share the name of a loved one to have their memory be commemorated during opening remarks at Tsukimi. Note: the floating lanterns are not for sale and can not be kept or taken. As this event will be taking place after dark (the Arboretum officially closes at sunset), please note that all guests must leave the grounds no later than 10pm. Guests are asked to be respectful of the grounds and of each other. Please abide by Arboretum rules - a

297.summary: PYGMALION: Nirosta Steel with Julianna Barwick + Mary Lattimore
297.description: Steven Hall, aka Nirosta Steel, presents My Skyscraper, an album that represents 40-years of works, reworks, and work-forever-in-progress. Friend, neighbor, collaborator, and co-conspirator of Arthur Russee; Hall is a sincere songwriting voice of the modern era. Julianna Barwick and Mary Lattimore join forces in Tragic Magic, a deeply atmospheric performance rooted in their acclaimed collaborative album created with the Philharmonie de Paris. Co-produced by Trevor Spencer, the music reflects an intuitive artistic connection forged over years of collaboration. Lattimore’s historically rich harp textures intertwine with Barwick’s layered vocals and analog synthesizers, including the Roland JUPITER and Prophet-5. Together, they create a contemplative sonic landscape that navigates grief, wonder, and renewal. Both intimate and expansive, the performance offers a moving meditation on human connection and the enduring, transformative power of artistic expression. Learn more about PYGMALION: Nirosta Steel with Julianna Barwick + Mary Lattimore

308.summary: 36th Annual Mortenson Distinguished Lecture - Jeff Chiba Stearns
308.description: 36th Annual Mortenson Distinguished Lecture ANIMATION MEDITATION: 25 Years of Exploring Mixed-Race Identity and Japanese Canadian History Through Visual Storytelling By Jeff Chiba Stearns Animation & Documentary Filmmaker | Author | Illustrator Hybrid Lecture & Book Signing Saturday, September 26, 2026; 1:00– 2:30 p.m. CT  I Hotel & Conference Center, Alma Mater Room; 1900 S. First Street, Champaign, ILThe Mortenson Center for International Library Programs is proud to bring Jeff Chiba Stearns to campus to present the 36th Annual Mortenson Distinguished Lecture and Youth Literarture Festival (YLF) Keynote during YLF Community Day. For more than two decades, Emmy-nominated and award-winning animation and documentary director, author, and illustrator Jeff Chiba Stearns has used visual storytelling to explore the intersections of Japanese Canadian history, mixed-race identity, family, and culture. Jeff will reflect on his creative journey—from his early animated and documentary films exploring what it means to be mixed-race and a fourth-generation Japanese Canadian, to his current work addressing these themes through children’s books and graphic novels.  Drawing from his projects such as One Big Hapa Family, Mixed Match, On Being Yukiko, Tomey: The Unyielding Spirit of Tomekichi Homma, and his latest graphic novel, Ojiichan’s Dragon, Jeff will share how his own experiences and family stories have shaped the subjects, characters, and worlds he creates. As a social justice advocate and educator, Jeff will discuss the importance of reclaiming and preserving Japanese Canadian stories, including the history of the more than 22,000 Japanese Canadians who were forcibly removed from their homes and incarcerated during the Second World War, and why this history remains relevant today.  Through behind-the-scenes stories, artwork, film clips, and personal reflections, Jeff will explore how a creative practice can evolve over 25 years—and how animation, illustration, comics, and f

309.description: Join us at the third annual Central Illinois Bat Festival — a free two-part celebration of bats, bugs, and science! This year, we’re celebrating backyard bugs and bats! Kicking off at 1pm at Anita Purves Nature Center, explore vendor booths, food trucks, kids art activities, face painting, and thrilling talks from top bat experts. Then, flap over to Crystal Lake Park at 5:30 kick things off with our costume contest of epic proportions for all ages. Contest starts at 6pm in the pavilion. All ages are welcome to enter; judging will be held by age groupings via applause-o-meter for fun bat-themed prizes.

315.summary: ONE PIECE Music Symphony with the Champaign-Urbana Symphony Orchestra
315.description: It is time to celebrate the ONE PIECE TV Series with an epic array of music full of action and emotion! Immerse yourself in the magic of a full orchestra as it performs One Piece’s iconic music live on stage, while the greatest moments from the anime come to life on screen in perfect sync. Relive more than 25 years of thrilling adventures of the Straw Hat crew, all set to the vibrant sounds of the series’ most memorable music! One Piece is the animated TV series adaption of creator Eiichiro Oda’s original manga. Produced by Toei Animation, this iconic TV series first debuted on Japanese TV in October 1999 and features pirate Monkey D. Luffy and his Straw Hat crew on their epic quest to find “The One Piece,” the legendary treasure of the former King of the Pirates, Gol D. Roger. Learn more about ONE PIECE Music Symphony with the Champaign-Urbana Symphony Orchestra

338.description: Join the Landuyt Center for Entrepreneurship this Spring 2027 as a Teaching Assistant supporting the Cozad New Venture Challenge and TE 598: Accelerating Deep Tech Enterprises. TAs will work alongside instructors, entrepreneurs, mentors, and student startup teams as they move ideas from early concepts toward viable ventures—gaining a front-row seat to entrepreneurship and innovation happening across the University of Illinois. 366.summary: Library Friends Exhibit : Celebrating Pride: 50+ Years of LGBTQ+ History at Illinois
366.description: Celebrate LGBTQ+ History Month by exploring 50+ years of LGBTQ+ student history at the University of Illinois! This exhibit brings together photographs, posters, newspaper clippings, archival records, and artifacts that tell the story of LGBTQ+ community, culture, and activism at Illinois.Discover the history of the Gay Illini, formed in 1975 and later recognized as an official Registered Student Organization, and learn about the continued legacy of LGBTQ+ communities at Illinois, including the launch of the University of Illinois Pride Alumni Network in 2025.During the week of Champaign-Urbana Pride Fest 2026, on October 16 at noon, join the University of Illinois Library and the University of Illinois Pride Alumni Network for a special Library Friends Webinar reflecting on 50 years of LGBTQ+ community, culture, and activism on campus and in the local community, find more information here. This webinar will feature Larry Cohen and Curtis McKay of the Illinois Pride Alumni Network; Siobhan B. Somerville, Associate Professor of English and Gender & Women's Studies; and Ellen D. Swain, Professor and Archivist for Student Life and Culture, University Library.
366.location: Display Cases near Main Stacks, Main Library, 1408 W. Gregory Drive, Urbana

404.summary: “Breathing Through the Roaring 2020s: Fascism, Imperial Breathlessness, and the Art of Breathing Otherwise” with Ronak K. Kapadia
404.description: What does it mean to breathe through the Roaring 2020s? Moving between the first Roaring Twenties and our own moment, Ronak K. Kapadia listens beneath the spectacle of crisis to the injuries and forms of support that public life increasingly trains us not to notice. Drawing from his book in progress, Breathing in Common, he traces the afterlives of US war-making into atmosphere, bodily capacity, and the infrastructures that sustain breath. Close readings of queer Pakistani artist Zulfikar Ali Bhutto and Nigerian American photographer Mikael Owunna show how contemporary art can reorganize exposure itself: sheltering bodies from compulsory visibility, rebuilding the conditions under which Black queer life appears, and making breathable life available as a problem of form.  Ronak K. Kapadia is an interdisciplinary scholar, writer, and curator whose work traces the aesthetic and material life of US empire and its violent afterlives, asking how minoritarian art makes those histories perceptible while creating other ways of sensing, knowing, and sustaining life. He is Associate Professor and Director of the Interdepartmental Graduate Concentration in Gender and Women’s Studies at the University of Illinois Chicago, with affiliations in Art History, Museum and Exhibition Studies, and Global Asian Studies.

426.summary: Do Rocky Exoplanets Retain Their Atmospheres?
426.description: The presence or absence of a planetary atmosphere is the outcome of a multi-billions-year long struggle between the planetary surface gravity, its outgassing rate, its magnetic field, and the stellar XUV and particle flux incident upon the world. The worlds found to transit nearby M-stars are more observationally accessible owing to the diminutive sizes and low luminosities of the central stars. However, recent work has demonstrated that these stars remain active and sustain high XUV fluxes for billions of years, much longer than the epoch of atmospheric production. With powerful infrared observatories in orbit and on the ground, we are now mapping the cosmic shoreline that separates airlines worlds from those with atmospheres, possibly even ones containing biosignature gases.

In a follow up to the September 15th Facilitating Dialogue around Objects of Hate, this program examines how visual artists create works that interrogate, reimagine, or repurpose objects and imagery associated with hate. 432.description: Since 1896, the Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra has been celebrated for artistic excellence,  innovation, and its deep commitment to community. Under the leadership of Music Director Manfred Honeck, now in his 19th season, the orchestra stands among the world’s finest, acclaimed for its precise sound, fresh interpretations, and renowned recordings. The Pittsburgh Symphony performs the work that earned them two Grammy Awards: Shostakovich’s Symphony No. 5. Composed under intense political scrutiny in Stalinist Russia, the work stands as a powerful and famously ambiguous response to oppression. The program opens with Carlos Simons’ Four Black American Dances, an exuberant and richly textured celebration of Black American musical traditions, followed by Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 2 featuring the commanding virtuosity and lyrical gifts of Yefim Bronfman. Learn more about Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra

435.summary: Healthy Animals, Resilient Farms: A Transatlantic Dialogue on Animal Health and Welfare
435.description: The Aspen Institute Germany, together with the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, is delighted to invite you to the virtual conference \"Healthy Animals, Resilient Farms: A Transatlantic Dialogue on Animal Health and Welfare\" on September 30, 2026 4:00 p.m. to 6:00 p.m. CEST/Berlin / 10:00 a.m. to 12:00 p.m. EST via Zoom.   How can Germany and the United States work together to shape the future of animal health and welfare in the swine and poultry industries? At a time of changing consumer expectations, growing biosecurity challenges, and increasing pressure on producers, the Transatlantic Dialogue on Animal Health and Welfare will bring together farmers, veterinarians, scientists, industry representatives, and policy makers from both sides of the Atlantic to discuss animal health and welfare in swine and poultry production. Besides exploring policies, practical approaches and opportunities for transatlantic cooperation, the event will highlight recommendations developed by the fourth U.S.-German Forum Future Agriculture cohort.  Confirmed speakers include Senator Thom Tillis, U.S. Senator for North Carolina, Ted McKinney, Chief Executive Officer of National Association of State Departments of Agriculture (NASDA) and former USDA Under Secretary for Trade and Foreign Agricultural Affairs, Dr. Franziska Kersten, Member of German Parliament and Member of the Committee on Agriculture, Food and Regional Identity and Dr. Katharina Kluge, Chief Veterinary Officer of Germany at the Ministry on Agriculture, Food and Regional Identity.  The event will be held in English. If you have any questions, please contact Ferdinand Eimler at eimler@aspeninstitute.de. We look forward to having you in the room for this important conversation!

448.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 449.summary: Stephanie O'Rourke | Landscapes of Dis-placement: Mining and Mapping the 19th-century British Empire
449.description: CAS Climate | Change Initiative: VICTORIAN CULTURE AND CLIMATE CHANGE SPEAKER SERIES. This lecture charts the emergence of new pictorial formats for representing landscape that derived from and accelerated industrial mineral extraction in Britain in the early 19th century. These formats, in turn, actively assimilated colonial environments in North America and India into a system of extractive capitalism through which Britain consolidated both economic and territorial power. In an alternative account of 19th-century landscape, Professor O’Rourke queries how pictorial formats alternately enabled or disabled this process.

460.description: Lunch Talk title: Sexual Harassment and the Geography of Service Work in the US “[At]…my first housekeeping job, I got discriminated because I was a heavyset woman…I thought I was doing good. At the end of the shift, they called me to the office. You're too big. You can't get on your knees and clean, so we don't need you.” Sheila Taylor, Room Attendant, Aria Hotel, Las Vegas, November 19, 2025 This presentation, which is pulled from the opening chapter of my working manuscript, Hands Off: A History of Fighting Back against Sexual Harassment in the American Workplace, explores the geography of the service sector. It follows two historical threads rooted in interdisciplinary theoretical frameworks. First, it introduces the reader to the physical spaces that that the workers (hospitality, flight attendants, and domestic workers) featured in this book occupy as they travel to and from work as well as where they labor. Second, by exploring the body as a geographical space, I provide a more theoretical framework of sexual harassment as I examine women’s bodies as a site of space through the literature on feminist cultural geography. The current scholarship of workplace-based gender violence is built on a framework that generally accepts the current neo-liberal capitalist system as the de facto reality and, by extension, the body becomes a space of abuse. With this book, I reject the constraints of our current institutions and their apparatuses as the default narrative. In the words of legal scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw, a study of workplace gender violence should not only be a “source of social empowerment” but also “reconstruction.” Building on recent scholarship, this chapter will scaffold the idea of “embodied intersectionality” demonstrating “…how the body can hold and express different identity attributes dependent on the everyday situations” of service work including race, age, migration background and gender, and also body size and appearance. 469.summary: MillerComm 2027 Lecture Series | \"Occupying America: War and the Infrastructure of US Power in a Globalizing World\" | Justin Jackson (University of Massachusetts, Amherst)
469.description: Presented by Justin Jackson (History, University of Massachusetts Amherst and George A. Miller Visiting Scholar in History). He will be working with the Center of Advanced Studies and the Department of History at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign this year. He will be co-organizing an April 2027 conference titled \"The Infrastructure of Empire, and the Empire of Infrastructure\". This conference will be sponsored by the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and the University of Birmingham (United Kingdom). Here is a link to Justin Jackson's Website: justinfjackson.com. This is A CAS MillerCom event hosted by the Department of History.  The US government’s deployment of troops to Chicago, Minneapolis and other cities, ostensibly to assist federal enforcement of immigration law, has vividly displayed its militarized infrastructure for policing one of globalization’s effects: transnational labor migration. In fact, the military occupation’s long if strange career across US history, from the British occupation of Boston to recent wars in Afghanistan and Iraq, suggests that occupying and globalizing have always been intertwined. Revolutionary-era Americans opposed occupation as tyranny. Yet the new United States almost immediately began resorting to military force and institutions to govern foreign and insurgent peoples, beginning with Native Americans, fugitives escaping slavery, and French and Spanish-speaking Americans. Despite its controversial politics, occupying became an indispensable technique of American power in a globalizing world, regulating growing flows of people, goods, and ideas that both weakened and strengthened US sovereignty at its peripheries. That occupying has come home to the North American heartland hints that the US government may be ever-more tempted to use the military to police and govern civilians and citizens as they confront rising crises of climate change, war, and mass migration. Hosted by: Department of History  In conjunct

492.description: Join the Center for Civic Education & Justice and the University YMCA for Friday Forum + Conversation Café! Each program features speakers, panels, or interactive conversations designed to inspire curiosity, critical thinking, and action.  Lunch is provided from the Y Thai Eatery at no cost, so come ready to eat, listen, learn, and join the conversation! This week's speaker: Olmeca In this lecture, Olmeca reflects on more than two decades of work across art, organizing, education, music, and community practice to explore a central question: what does it mean to live rebellion, not only resist? Drawing from lived experience, ancestral knowledge, cultural memory, and social movements, Olmeca examines Radical Love as responsibility transformed into action—through protest, teaching, art-making, care, spirituality, collective work, and joy. The lecture considers how everyday practices can become acts of resistance, how ancestral knowledge continues to shape the future, and how joy itself can become an act of rebellion in systems that depend on isolation, dispossession, and powerlessness. 498.description: Shiv Priyam Raghuraman is an assistant Professor in the Department of Climate, Meteorology & Atmospheric Sciences (CliMAS) at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign (UIUC).  How Earth gains and loses energy is key to its habitability because perturbations to the planetary radiation balance alters the entire climate system. Clouds, aerosols, greenhouse gases, land, ocean, and ice, all interact with radiation. Therefore, changes in these constituents manifest as radiative changes at the top-of-the-atmosphere observable from space. We now not only have continuous satellite observations, but also climate models that represent the Earth system better than ever before.  My research program takes full advantage of this unprecedented and timely opportunity to provide physical mechanisms and theories that explain how these radiative changes cause Earth to accumulate heat. Clouds are central to Earth’s heat budget as they cover two-thirds of the planet. My research not only provides a process-based understanding of how radiation responds to clouds, but also how clouds respond to surface warming, leading to a holistic understanding of the feedback loop.   Priyam's CliMAS Faculty page

505.summary: Cynthia Oliver Company Dance Theatre presents Turn. Turning. TURNT
505.description: Turn. Turning. TURNT  is a compelling triptych by award-winning Dance at Illinois professor, choreographer, and director Dr. Cynthia Oliver that captures movement, memory, and resilience across three distinct yet interconnected works. Tether  draws on AfroFuturist imagination and the cultural practice of double Dutch driven by Black girls’ creativity and aspiration. Fallow  reflects the urgency and adaptability required to navigate constant uncertainty, while Summon. Sow. Reap  contemplates the outcomes of collective labor—both just and unjust—through reflection and renewal. This richly layered performance is brought to life by a cast of Dance at Illinois alumni and an accomplished team of collaborators, blending choreography, music, visual art, and design into a dynamic sensory experience. Oliver’s global perspective and scholarly depth infuse the work with emotional and cultural resonance. TURNT  ultimately invites audiences to witness a powerful journey of recovery, remembrance, and reimagining—an artistic call to return, rebuild, and move forward with renewed purpose. Please note, this performance includes occasional expletives. Learn more about Cynthia Oliver Company Dance Theatre presents Turn. Turning. TURNT

521.summary: CEAPS Speaker | \"Self-Determination in Very Small Places\" | Bradley Simpson (University of Connecticut)
521.description: Join us for our first speaker event of the semester. About the Talk: The idea of self-determination is one of the most significant in modern international politics. For more than a century, diplomats, lawyers, scholars, activists, and ordinary people in every part of the globe have wrestled with its meaning and implications for decolonization, human rights, sovereignty, and international order. The First Right (Oxford UP, 2025) argues that there was no one version of self-determination, but a century-long contest between contending visions of sovereignty and rights. Brad Simpson will focus in this talk on those places that were considered too small, too backwards, or too primitive to self-determination, and their implications for contemporary global politics.  About the Speaker: Brad Simpson is Professor of History and Asian Studies at the University of Connecticut. He is the author of Economists with Guns: Authoritarian Development and US-Indonesian Relations, 1960-1968. His new book is The First Right: Self-Determination and the Transformation of International Order, 1941-2000.  https://www.bradleyrsimpson.com/

524.summary: Brown Bag Series- Ensuring Non-Interference, Maintaining Resilient Democracy: Contemporary Challenges in Legislation on Countering Covert Foreign Influence y Maxim Krupskiy
524.description: Ensuring Non-Interference, Maintaining Resilient Democracy: Contemporary Challenges in Legislation on Countering Covert Foreign Influence Nowadays, legislation on countering foreign interference is a double-edged sword—it is successfully used by autocratic and illiberal actors to suppress dissent, while at the same time being developed by many democratic actors as a tool to protect against malicious foreign influence. At times, the rhetoric used by proponents of this legislation on both sides is difficult to distinguish, and its potential risks lie in the details. The purpose of this presentation is to discuss pressing challenges related to the development of legislation on countering foreign interference and, drawing on the case law of the European Court of Human Rights and the expert opinions of the Venice Commission, to attempt to answer the question of how democracies can protect themselves from covert, malicious foreign influence without compromising their resilience.BIO: Maxim Krupskiy is a human rights defender, attorney-at-law, research scholar and Ph.D. in Philosophy with more than twelve years of litigation in Russia defending refugees, civil activists persecuted by the Russian authorities, and NGOs labeled as so-called “foreign agents” for political reasons. He is a former visiting scholar at the Fletcher School of Law and Diplomacy at Tufts University, former non-resident fellow at the The George Washington University and former research scholar at The Kennan Institute of the Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars (Galina Starovoitova Fellowship on Human Rights and Conflict Resolution). Currently he is a research scholar at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. He is conducting a comprehensive comparative research on legislation countering foreign interference, specifically the “foreign agent” laws, within the frameworks of autocratic legalism and resilient democracy. He teaches two courses at UIUC: “Contemporary Autocracy in Theory,

535.description: Decoding the Pet Microbiome: From Lab Tools to Real Life Impact We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Jonathan Turck from Texas A&M University.  Date: Tuesday, October 6, 2026  Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online WebinarJonathan Turck is a third-year PhD student and Bioinformatics Graduate Research Assistant at the Gastrointestinal Laboratory at Texas A&M University. He earned his Bachelor’s degree in Biology with a minor in Bioinformatics from Texas A&M, and his research combines biological and data-driven approaches to better understand the pet microbiome. His work focuses on microbial bioinformatics and the development of machine learning-based biomarkers aimed at improving clinical care and advancing reproducible microbiome testing.The pet microbiome has become one of the fastest-growing areas in animal health and nutrition research, but understanding how laboratory findings translate into practical applications can be challenging. In this session, Jonathan will explore the tools and technologies used to study the microbiome, discuss how data science and machine learning are shaping the field, and highlight how these discoveries may impact future approaches to companion animal health and clinical care. 537.summary: As the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope Graduates from Construction to Discoveries
537.description: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope launched on August 30, 2026. This flagship mission’s vast, deep surveys will help astronomers explore dark matter, dark energy, exoplanets, and almost anything from our own solar system to galaxies at the edge of the observable universe. The telescope provides the sharpness and sensitivity of Hubble, but with its 300-megapixel camera it can map the cosmos a thousand times faster. Commissioning is now underway, and beginning in early 2027 Roman will begin producing a wealth of survey observations. The data – almost 1.5TB of images per day – will be released in near-real-time to accelerate the rate of astronomical discoveries.

549.summary: CLACS & CEAPS Present: Narratives of youth, violence and drugs. Comparing “mano dura” in Ecuador and the Philippines
549.description: On October 7th at 3PM in Coble Hall Room 306, CLACS and the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies are excited to present Cristina Cielo's talk, \"Narratives of youth, violence and drugs. Comparing “mano dura” in Ecuador and the Philippines\" The US led global campaign for the “War on Drugs” has had severe consequences throughout the global South. Among these impacts is the criminalization of marginal populations, particularly young men, which has provided justification for security responses ranging from militarization to extra-judicial killings to selective disappearances. This paper examines the role that the figure of youth plays in government rhetoric justifying strong hand measures to battle drug trade in Ecuador and the Philippines. The two country’s radically different discourses on youth in their drug wars allows us to understand that specific national constructions of disposable populations are articulated with US influence in global political economies. Even after its independence, the Philippines has served as a US geopolitical outpost and its drug war takes on protective characteristics that legitimize state violence against suspected drug users in order to “save our youth”. The drug war in Latin America, in contrast, has identified more direct targets for US deployment of political and enforcement strategies and resources. In the Ecuadorian narratives that justify increased military and police presence, government and media representations of youth focus on racialized young men as criminals. Recently, a law was enacted that increases punitive measures in Ecuador’s youth justice system. A comparative examination of the figure of young people in the Philippines and Ecuador’s state responses to violence and drugs sheds light on the construction of \"internal enemies\" in the contexts of postcolonial and imperial inequalities.Cristina Cielo is a Professor in the Department of Sociology and Gender Studies at the Facultad Latinoamericana de Ciencias Socia

551.summary: Faculty Job Search: Dual Career Considerations
551.description: For those in long-term relationships, the faculty job search presents additional layers of complexity and anxiety: balancing career and personal priorities, navigating competing career needs, addressing partner hires in negotation, and more. In the first 30 minutes of this session, the presenter will outline major dual career considerations for a faculty job search. The remaining 30 minutes will be devoted to questions and conversation to get you the answers you need going forward. This workshop is relevant for those in relationships with one academic or with multiple academics.No registration required. Students will leave the workshop with (1) basic knowledge about research proposals and their structure, (2) tactics and tools to write successful research statements, and (3) a list of resources for assistance in the writing process. This workshop is a collaboration between the Office of Undergraduate Research and the Writers Workshop and will be most well-suited for undergraduates who are drafting proposals for the first time, hoping to improve their proposal writing skills, and/or applying for an OUR Research Support Grant. These artists rose to moment, producing powerful works of art and political commentary that sought more humane and equitable futures for all. There are strong parallels between our current crisis in human rights and these historical precedents. In Search of a Future invites audiences to consider these connections, and to use this exhibition as a space for collective reflection and dialogue about the capacity of art to reveal difficult truths and dare us to build more just futures. Curated by Kathryn Koca Polite. On view through May 15.  Museum Hours: Tue–Fri 10–5 | Sat 10–4 | Thu until 8 pm  Parking nearby is free after 5 pm and on weekends. 567.summary: Food For Thought | Nicholas Jackson and Stefan Vogler
567.description: Food for Thought: A series of public events featuring research and creative projects by recent CAS Associates and Fellows. We are delighted to showcase the work of some of our most productive and creative faculty in this informal series of intellectually and spiritually invigorating presentations. You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty. 11:00am-11:45am: Nicholas Jackson, CAS Fellow 2025-26, Chemistry More information to come!  Noon-12:45pm: Stefan Vogler, CAS Fellow 2025-26, Sociology Police Consciousness and the Potential for Reform This talk develops the concept of “police consciousness” to explore how people understand policing either as a collective of autonomous individuals or as an institution with systemic influence. Drawing on a nationally representative survey of both LGBTQ and non-LGBTQ people and in-depth interviews with 59 LGBTQ survey respondents, Professor Vogler shows that this individual-institutional divide shapes attitudes toward police legitimacy and reform preferences. Those with institutional views are more likely to support more transformative and structural reforms, while those with more individualistic perspectives tend to favor reformist efforts focused on improving officers through things like training and weeding out “bad apples,” and these understandings and preferences are shaped by social identities.
567.location: Levis Faculty Center, Room 208, 919 W Illinois St

570.description: Discussion with the author (Justin Jackson) of \"An Army of Workmen: The Politics of Military-Colonial Public Works,\" chap. 3 of The Work of Empire: War, Occupation, and the Making of American Colonialism in Cuba and the Philippines (University of North Carolina Press, 2025).  This chapter of The Work of Empire, a study of how Cubans' and Filipinos' labor for the US military between the Spanish-American War and World War I affected American colonialism and these nations' histories, explores the politics and political economy road-building in these war-torn islands, under US military occupation. While US occupiers coerced and recruited Cubans and Filipinos to build streets and highways to facilitate military and police mobility, sanitation, and economic recovery, Cuban and Filipino elites and laborers seized infrastructure's politics of taxation and revenue to turn the logic of empire-building against US policy aims. The result were infrastructural states in Cuba and the Philippines that empowered Cubans and Filipinos to resist labor coercion and adapt the political economy of public works to their own ends.

571.summary: The Rule of Law - Presented by Chief Justice P. Scott Neville, Jr., Illinois Supreme Court
571.description: The Rule of Law Presented by Chief Justice P. Scott Neville, Jr., Illinois Supreme CourtOur democracy endures as long as the rule of law remains understood, trusted, and shared. A distinguished jurist and longtime advocate for equal justice, Chief Justice Neville is committed to making Illinois Courts serve as “a national model” that safeguards equal justice for all, regardless of identity, geography, or resources.This event is free and open to the public. A limited number of lunches will be provided to attendees.About Chief Justice Neville Chief Justice P. Scott Neville, Jr. is the 123rd Chief Justice of the Illinois Supreme Court and the second Black Chief Justice in Illinois history. He has served on the Illinois Supreme Court since 2018. He previously served on the Illinois Appellate Court as well as the Circuit Court of Cook County. Over the course of Chief Justice Neville's 52-year legal career he has worked with public and private entities, held leadership roles in numerous bar and judicial organizations, and received awards and appointments in recognition of his service and leadership. A product of Chicago's public schools, he earned his undergraduate degree from Culver-Stockton College and his law degree from Washington University School of Law.

574.summary: Up Against Erasure | Nanna Bonde Thylstrup: “Staying with the Trouble of Preservation: The Ambivalent Politics of Deletion in Digital Societies”
574.description: Nanna Bonde Thylstrup is Associate Professor of Digital Culture at the University of Copenhagen and Principal Investigator of the multi-year project Data Loss: the Politics of Disappearance, Destruction and Dispossession in Digital Societies (DALOSS) funded by the European Research Council. Her research examines the politics and ethics of data, machine learning and digital infrastructures, with a particular interest in how digitization and algorithmic processes are changing how we encounter, govern and practice knowledge and its infrastructures. She is the author of The Politics of Mass Digitization (MIT Press, 2018), and co-editor of Uncertain Archives: Critical Keywords for Big Data (MIT Press, 2021) and (W)ARCHIVES: Archival Imaginaries, War, and Contemporary Art (Sternberg Press, 2021). Her writing has appeared in venues ranging from Big Data & Society to the New York Times. She has held visiting fellowships at Duke, Cornell and Columbia, and serves as the humanities representative in the University of Copenhagen's Quantum Hub Network.

575.summary: Krannert Center Uncorked with CU Folk & Roots Festival: Dan Kusaya & The Chimurenga Inspiration
575.description: Dan Kusaya & The Chimurenga Inspiration bring the vibrant sounds of Zimbabwe to Krannert Center Uncorked in a joyful, high-energy celebration of music and culture to kick off the 2026 CU Folk & Roots Festival! Led by Zimbabwean-born musician Dan Kusaya, this seven-piece Champaign-Urbana ensemble blends the hypnotic sounds of the mbira and marimba with the infectious rhythms of chimurenga, Afrobeat, reggae, jazz, and dance music. The result is a sound that honors Zimbabwean heritage while incorporating other musical traditions to create something wholly unique. Rooted in themes of resilience, unity, and cultural pride, the band's performances invite audiences to dance, connect, and celebrate. Whether delivering meditative Shona mbira melodies, driving Afrobeat grooves, or soulful jazz-infused rhythms, Dan Kusaya & The Chimurenga Inspiration create an experience that is as uplifting as it is unforgettable. Come see why they have earned the title, \"The most original vibe in the Midwest.\" Enjoy a beverage from the Stage 5 Bar, connect with friends old and new, and be prepared to dance! All Krannert Center Uncorked performances are free at Stage 5 in the Krannert Center lobby. Learn more about this year's CU Folk and Roots Festival at https://FolkAndRoots.org Learn more about Krannert Center Uncorked with CU Folk & Roots Festival: Dan Kusaya & The Chimurenga Inspiration

Starting at 7 p.m., participants will hit the course decked out in bright race shirts, glow-in-the-dark gear, and plenty of Illini spirit as we illuminate the night together. Whether you're chasing a personal record, jogging with friends, or enjoying a leisurely walk, this timed 5K welcomes runners and walkers of all ages and ability levels. The atmosphere is casual, energetic, and family-friendly, making it the perfect event for seasoned athletes and first-time participants alike. Best of all, your participation supports a great cause. 578.description: Have a great idea, invention, or startup—and wondering how to protect it? Join Professor Joe Barich for an engaging and practical introduction to intellectual property (IP) designed specifically for entrepreneurs and innovators. Professor Barich will break down the fundamentals of patents, trademarks, and other forms of IP; explain what they protect and why they matter; and highlight common mistakes that can cause entrepreneurs to lose valuable rights. You’ll learn how patents can protect inventions, how trademarks safeguard your company and brand, and how intellectual property can become an important asset as a venture grows. With more than 25 years of experience as a patent and trademark attorney and extensive experience teaching entrepreneurs at the University of Illinois, Professor Barich makes a complex topic approachable, relevant, and useful for anyone developing a new idea or business.

585.summary: Breaking Chains, Building Futures: Pathways to Redemption, Education, & Excellence
585.description: Join the Center for Civic Education & Justice and the University YMCA for Friday Forum + Conversation Café! This lunchtime series creates space to learn from diverse perspectives, engage in thoughtful dialogue, and connect with others across differences. Each program features speakers, panels, or interactive conversations designed to inspire curiosity, critical thinking, and action. Lunch is provided from the Y Thai Eatery at no cost, so come ready to eat, listen, learn, and join the conversation! This week's speaker: Dr. Stanley Andrisse Stanley Andrisse is an endocrinologist, scientist, educator, author, and social justice advocate whose powerful personal journey informs his work to expand access to education and opportunity. After being sentenced to 10 years in a maximum-security prison, Dr. Andrisse went on to earn his Ph.D. and M.B.A. and build a career in science and higher education. Through his research, advocacy, mentorship, and lived experience, he challenges assumptions about incarceration, education, and who is given the opportunity to thrive. His work highlights the transformative power of education while calling attention to the systemic barriers that justice-impacted individuals continue to face, bringing a powerful and deeply personal perspective to conversations about second chances, equity, opportunity, and the potential that can be unlocked when people are given the support and resources to pursue new possibilities.
585.location: University YMCA, 1001 S. Wright St., Champaign

621.description: Not Your Mascot: The Impact of (Mis)RepresentationThis year's Indigenous Peoples' Day theme explores the ongoing struggle for Indigenous peoples to be seen, heard, and represented on their own terms. Native American mascots, logos, and stereotypical imagery are not isolated symbols. Instead, they are manifestations of a broader colonial legacy that has long reduced Indigenous peoples to caricatures while obscuring Native sovereignty, humanity, diversity, and the contemporary existence of Tribal Nations (IllumiNative, 2023; National Congress of American Indians [NCAI], 2020). For decades, Tribal Nations, Native organizations, scholars, students, and community leaders have advocated for the retirement of Native mascots and imagery that perpetuate harmful stereotypes. Yet these representations continue to be defended as symbols of tradition, pride, or honor, often dismissing Indigenous voices and minimizing the documented harms such imagery causes. Research has demonstrated that Native mascots negatively influence the psychological well-being and identity development of Native youth while reinforcing racial stereotypes among Native and non-Native audiences (Fryberg et al., 2008). Native-led advocacy organizations, including the National Indian Health Board (2024), have further identified Native mascots as both a public health and social justice issue because of their harmful effects on Native identity, belonging, and community well-being. This event is open to all eligible persons regardless of race, color, or national origin. Reasonable accommodations are available upon request, please contact nah@illinois.edu.

654.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 696.summary: Up Against Erasure | Faculty Reading: Ángel García
696.description: Professor Ángel García (English/Creative Writing) will read from his latest collection, Indifferent Cities. About Indifferent Cities: Through one state to another, from one country to the next, Indifferent Cities traverses both distance and time to reconcile the most confounding reality of family: our people, sometimes, are the people we know least. Utilizing forms such as ekphrasis and epistolary, the collection sources photographs, postcards, and official documents as well as rumor, suspicion, and supposition to uncover the consequences, by choice or circumstance, of migration and immigration between Mexico and the United States across four generations. Surveying the terrain of what one knows and does not know, what one inherits and disinherits, Indifferent Cities wrestles with every departure, each arrival, and the author’s inevitable return to determine where and to who he belongs. About the speaker: Ángel García, the proud son of Mexican immigrants, is the author of Indifferent Cities (Tupelo Press), winner of a Helena Whitehill Book award, and Teeth Never Sleep (University of Arkansas Press), recipient of a CantoMundo Poetry Prize, an American Book Award, and finalist for a PEN America Open Book Award and a Kate Tufts Award. His work has been published in the American Poetry Review, McSweeney's, Crab Orchard Review, Huizache, The Acentos Review, Michigan Quarterly Review, Adroit Journal, and most recently in Mānoa: A Pacific Journal of International Writing and Gulf Coast. The recipient of fellowships from CantoMundo, Community of Writers, Vermont Studio Center, and MacDowell, Ángel is currently an associate professor of English and teaches in the MFA Program at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign.

Sitar maestro Niladri Kumaar is hailed as a maverick musician and composer, a celebrated ambassador, and an Indian music icon who frequently collaborated with Hussain over many years. Kumaar returns to Krannert Center with his program The Space Between the Notes, honoring the iconic Hussain and their shared musical tradition. The Space Between the Notes is a musical journey rooted in tradition, and sure to deeply resonate with the hearts of music fans around the world. 708.summary: CEAPS Speaker/Political Science Workshop | \"Is Soft Power a Zero-Sum Competition?\" | Austin Strange (Associate Professor of International Relations, Department of Politics and Public Administration, University of Hong Kong)
708.description: Abstract: Is soft power zero-sum? Is one state’s soft power gain inevitably another’s loss? Academic and policy debates, particularly on intensifying US-China competition, often adopt a zero-sum logic for analyzing soft power. Yet this assumption, apparently borrowed from classic theories of “hard” power transitions, has received little conceptual or empirical scrutiny. We study whether states can possess different types of positive reputation that can increase their soft power in specific domains or issue areas without necessarily diminishing the soft power of other states. Empirically, we examine this possibility in American and Chinese overseas development finance programs, which are popularly seen as having distinct reputations. Using an original survey experiment in Thailand, we test whether and how American- and Chinese-sponsored development activities reflecting different reputational elements affect views toward both governments. The findings show when soft power is built on a reputation for being a principled actor who does things the right way, it is generally perceived as zero-sum. However, when soft power is instead based on a reputation for being competent at completing concrete tasks, zero-sum perceptions weaken. Our findings deepen efforts to theorize soft power by illuminating conditions under which soft power competition may be more and less intense. Biography: Austin Strange is an Associate Professor of International Relations in the Department of Politics and Public Administration at the University of Hong Kong, where he directs the Master of International and Public Affairs (MIPA) program. He researches and teaches international relations, international development, and Chinese foreign policy. He is the author of Chinese Global Infrastructure (Cambridge University Press) and co-author of Banking on Beijing: The Aims and Impacts of China’s Overseas Development Program (Cambridge University Press). At HKU he received the Early Career Teaching Award

717.summary: Improvisers Exchange Workshop: Anida Yoeu Ali Performance for Non-Dancers
717.description: Performance for Non-Dancers: Performance is doing, being, acting and dancing. This workshop is designed for participants who do not necessarily identify as dancers and/or who have minimal or no experience with performance. In this studio-based workshop, we will learn how to hone presence and transform ordinary gestures into creative extraordinary performances. Participants will grow their awareness and appreciation of movement in all its diverse forms as well as their ability to communicate through non-verbal expression. We will learn to select, develop, and perform everyday human actions into dancelike movement and/or performance action. We will explore our emotional, intellectual, and kinesthetic selves while learning the elements that make up performance: time, space and energy. Improvisers Exchange programming is supported by Krannert Center for the Performing Arts and University of Illinois School of Music. Open to All, Admission Free Anida Yoeu Ali (b. 1974, Battambang, Cambodia) is an interdisciplinary artist whose works span performance, installation, new media, public encounters, and political agitation. Born in Cambodia and raised in Chicago, she is a first-generation American of mixed Malay, Cham, Khmer, and Thai ancestries. Working transnationally, Ali investigates the artistic, spiritual, and political collisions of her diasporic, hybrid identity with the resolve that in-betweenness is a powerful space for creation and provocation. Ali believes performance allows for a magic of reinventing the self and projecting “larger-than-life” personas liberated from oppressive representations. Currently based in Tacoma, Ali is also the co-founder of Studio Revolt, an independent artist-run media lab whose works have agitated the White House, won awards at film festivals, and redefined what it means to create sans studio and trans-nomadically. Ali’s works have been acquired by public and private collections and globally exhibited, including at Haus der Kunst, Palai

746.summary: Workshop on Nuclear Energy and Applications
746.description: Nuclear energy has always advanced through a steady pairing of fundamentals with practical engineering: reactor physics and materials, instrumentation and controls, licensing and operations. This workshop follows that tradition while looking ahead to the systems and enabling technologies shaping the next generation of fission and fusion deployments. Across two full days of invited and contributes talks and moderated discussions, participants will connect core concepts to real-world pathways: technology options, supply chains and qualification, monitoring and safeguards, digitalization, grid integration, and the social and workforce foundations needed for durable progress.Topics include:Nuclear power fundamentals and technology pathways (fission and fusion context)Industry–university perspectives on development, testing, qualification, and scale-upAdvanced-reactor applications and missions (including non-electric and specialized deployments)Reactor monitoring, sensors, and measurement strategies; safeguards readinessRegulatory landscape, standards, and the role of professional societiesDigital twins, modeling and simulation, data analytics, and AI for design and operationsEnergy storage and grid integration; hybrid systems and load-following considerationsSocial, ethical, and workforce dimensions that support durable deployment

752.summary: AsiaLENS | \"THOSE4YEARS\" Free Screening & Discussion with Filmmaker Dr Joe Thomas Karackattu
752.description: Synopsis: The film is an amazing journey into the lives of those Chinese who came to India around the middle of the 19th century… speaking a language unknown to their neighbours when they first arrived. It journeys across three countries and reams of colonial office records to retrace the places those people came from, the means and mode of their arrival, and how many of them ended up making India their home. It is a history of people, plants and places - as it catalogues their contributions to plantations, locates places and sites associated with their earliest arrival and stay and, more remarkably, manages to locate some of the descendants of those Chinese who arrived in India over 150 years ago. The film is based on fieldwork in Hong Kong, Malaysia and Southern India. It has been screened in the United States (Penn State University, University of Pittsburgh, New School), The United Kingdom ( King's College, SOAS University of London), UAE, Qatar, China (Tsinghua University, Beijing Foreign Studies University), Malaysia (Universiti Malaya) and across India. (52 minutes)   Trailer: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1Ox7R2pTqe0   About the Filmmaker:Dr Joe Thomas Karackattu is a Professor with the Humanities and Social Sciences Department at IIT Madras. He was a Fox Fellow (2008–2009) at Yale University, Centenary Visiting Fellow (2013) at SOAS, University of London and CISLI Fellow with the India-China Institute at the New School, New York (2017-19). Joe studied Economics at St. Stephen's College (Delhi) and Chinese studies at Jawaharlal Nehru University (Delhi). He was awarded the \"Srimathi Marti Annapurna Gurunath Award for Excellence in Teaching\" 2024 from IIT Madras, and was previously recipient of the \"Young Faculty Recognition Award\" 2020 at IIT Madras. Besides publishing two books and several journal papers, Prof Karackattu has also made two non-fiction films on India-China relations, which have been screened across top universities globally.
