761.summary: Relativistic Stellar Explosions: The Landscape Revealed by Wide-field, High-cadence Optical Surveys
761.description: For the last half-century, relativistic outflows accompanying the final collapse of massive stars have predominantly been detected via high-energy emission, as long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs). However, it has long been hypothesized that GRBs are the extreme of a continuum of phenomena, including dirty fireballs and off-axis jets. I will show that the large grasp of optical surveys has recently made it possible to test this hypothesis by probing the phase space of fast and rare transients, with targeted radio observations playing a crucial role in confirming the presence of relativistic ejecta. I will review the emerging zoo, which includes orphan afterglows at cosmological distances, radio-bright supernovae in the local universe, and unexpected new classes of transients that are prime targets for millimeter-band observations. An understanding of the origin of these events and their relation to GRBs will be enabled by upcoming time-domain surveys in other bands, such as X-ray and UV.

771.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 799.summary: Islam in France: Minority Religion, Laïcité, and the Politics of Muslim Identity
799.description: This lecture treats Islam in France as a case study in the state management of minority religion in a secular republic. Three interrelated dimensions structure the discussion. First, French laïcité is examined as a singular and frequently misunderstood normative framework, whose logic and historical genealogy differ substantially from American models of church-state separation. Second, it addresses the question of radicalization and deradicalization, drawing on fieldwork conducted in French prison settings, including units specifically dedicated to radicalized inmates (Quartiers de Prise en Charge de la Radicalisation). Third, the lecture engages with contemporary debates on Muslim identity in a postcolonial context, and in particular the question of religious authority: who speaks for Islam in France, and on what grounds? Together, these three dimensions illuminate the specific tensions that shape the lives of Muslim communities in contemporary Western Europe.  Hosted by: Department of History In conjunction with: Center for African Studies, Center for Global Studies, Center for South American & Middle Eastern Studies, Department of Religion, European Union Center, Humanities Research Institute

851.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 865.summary: Up Against Erasure | Faculty Book Talk: Gillen D'Arcy Wood
865.description: Professor Gillen D'Arcy Wood (English and Earth Science & Environmental Change) will discuss his book, The Wake of HMS Challenger: How a Legendary Victorian Voyage Tells the Story of Our Oceans’ Decline. The book received the 2026 Watson, Helen, Miles, and Audrey Davis Prize from the History of Science Society. The prize honors books in the history of science directed to a wide public.About the speaker: Gillen D'Arcy Wood is Robert W. Schaefer Professor of Liberal Arts and Sciences at UIUC, where he is founding director of the undergraduate Certificate in Environmental Writing. His 2014 book Tambora (Princeton) won the Kendrick Prize from the Society for Literature, Science, and the Arts, while his most recent book project, The Wake of HMS Challenger (Princeton) was awarded a Carnegie Fellowship and the Davis Prize by the History of Science Society in 2026. He is the author of four other books and numerous articles on nineteenth-century culture, science, and environmental history. His new research focuses on seabirds and biodiversity heritage islands.About the The Wake of HMS Challenger: In December 1872, HMS Challenger embarked on the first round-the-world oceanographic expedition. Its goal: to shine a light for the first time on the mysteries of the deep sea. For the next four years, Challenger’s naturalists explored the oceans, encountering never-before-seen marvels of marine life. The expedition’s achievements are the stuff of legend. It identified major ocean currents and defining features of the seafloor, including the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and Mariana Trench. It measured worldwide sea temperatures and chemistry, creating baseline data for all ocean research since. And, most spectacularly of all, it collected nearly five thousand sea creatures and plants new to science. 878.description: Get up to speed on using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide to make Canvas pages more accessible for everyone! In this hands-on workshop, we’ll start with an overview of the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide, how it functions, what the various errors, alerts, structural elements, and features mean, and how to fix these issues on a Canvas page. Then we’ll jump into some hands-on practice using the Canvas Accessibility Guide to evaluate the accessibility of Canvas pages and remediate basic accessibility issues. 879.summary: Book Talk: Professor Sanjay Joshi, \"Brahmins of the Himalaya\"
879.description: Brahmins of the Himalaya: Upper Caste Ways of Belonging 1850-1950 (Permanent Black and SUNY Press, 2026) draws on a rich archive of family letters, including letters by women, and challenges the idea that the everyday can be conflated with the trivial.  Through a focus on the quotidian, Brahmins seeks to challenge the master narratives that have long dominated the history of the subcontinent. Sanjay Joshi teaches South Asian History at Northern Arizona University and serves as the Ashraf B. Nasir Fellow in the Honors College. He received his BA and MA from the University of Delhi and a Ph.D. in Modern South Asian History from the University of Pennsylvania. He is the author of Fractured Modernity: Making of a Middle Class in Colonial North India (Oxford University Press, 2001) and the editor of The Middle Class in Colonial India (Oxford University Press, 2010).

884.summary: Timbuktu Talks: Islam in Africa: Between Sufism, Salafism, and Indigenous Religious Authority
884.description: This lecture examines the case of Chérif Ousmane Madani Haïdara and the Ançar Dine movement in Mali as a window into the dynamics of contemporary African Islam. The main argument is that figures like Haïdara articulate a theology of resistance, one that pushes back simultaneously against radical Islamism and against ‘‘imported’’ forms of Islam, whether Wahhabi or Arab-centric in orientation. This lecture will engage broader questions of religious authority, the decolonization of Islamic knowledge, and the plurality of Muslim identities in Sub-Saharan Africa.  This will be a hybrid event. Please register to receive the Zoom link.  Youssouf Sangaré is a George A. Miller Visiting Scholar. He is a scholar of Islamic studies specializing in modern and contemporary Muslim thought. He is currently Associate Professor (Maître de conférences) in Islamic Studies at the Institut national des langues et civilisations orientales - INALCO (Paris), where he also serves as Director of the Master's program in Arabic Studies and Co-Director of the Diploma in Islamic Studies. His work sits at the intersection of Islamic theology, hermeneutics, and the intellectual history of the Muslim world, with a particular focus on reformist thinkers and on the reinterpretation of Islamic sources by both classical and contemporary scholars.

Mowry is a Curator of Rare Books and Manuscripts and Assistant Professor at the Rare Book & Manuscript Library, University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. 919.summary: Crowds as Scarce Resource: Collective Behavior in Early Medieval Europe -- Prof. Shane Bobrycki (University of Iowa)
919.description: Historians have studied crowds and collective behavior in many settings. Early Medieval Europe (c. 500-1000) presents a unique chapter in crowd history, when logistical constraints on gatherings were comparatively high, thanks to post-Roman demographic and urban decline. Nevertheless, imperatives to assemble remained strong, in societies that used gatherings to exchange information and things, saw numbers as proof of legitimacy, and envisioned themselves as heirs to crowd-filled ancient Rome. It is a setting in which crowds look and act very differently from other periods studied by crowd history (among other things, there was no fixed word for \"riot\"). How can the history of the crowd as a scarce resource inform medievalists, both of Europe and of other regions? What might it offer to scholars of crowds in other settings?   Please join us for this talk by Professor Shane Bobrycki (University of Iowa), author of The Crowd in the Early Middle Ages (2024).

926.summary: Helping Pets Thrive with Plasma: A Multifaceted Ingredient Providing Health, Nutrition & Processing Benefits
926.description: Helping Pets Thrive with Plasma: A Multifaceted Ingredient Providing Health, Nutrition & Processing Benefits We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Dr. Joy Campbell, Global Pet Food Technical Service Lead at APC. Date: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online Webinar Dr. Campbell earned her Ph.D. in Nutritional Sciences from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign and has spent more than 20 years leading research and development efforts at APC. Her work focuses on the role of functional proteins in animal health and nutrition, helping develop innovative products used across multiple animal species. Plasma-based ingredients offer a unique opportunity to improve pet foods, treats, and supplements through a combination of nutritional, health, and processing benefits. In this webinar, Dr. Campbell will discuss how these ingredients support the wellbeing of cats and dogs and contribute to high-quality pet nutrition. Founded in 1981, APC is the global leader in plasma-derived functional proteins for animal nutrition. Through decades of research and innovation, APC develops ingredients that support animal health and are used in diets that positively impact billions of animals worldwide. APC employs more than 500 people across 8 countries and operates 18 manufacturing facilities, all guided by a passion for helping animals thrive. This webinar is generously supported by APC. 936.summary: Reception & MillerComm Lecture Series | \"The Journey of Yao's Black Divine Comedy\" | Yao Jui-Chung in Dialogue with Kao Chen-Hui
936.description: Please join us for... 4:00pm - 5:00pm Reception with light refreshments, hosted by UAAT Mandarin Education Program Liaison Office for the University of Illinois System  5:00pm - 6:30pm MillerComm Lecture with Yao Jui-Chung in Dialogue with Kao Chen-Hui About the Lecture Every landscape is a storyscape, shaped by narratives beyond its borders and beneath its surface. How can art reveal concealed histories and reshape what it means to belong to a place? If the land could speak, how would it tell its own story—and how might its gaze unsettle our own? For over three decades, Taiwanese artist Yao Jui-Chung has worked across media to explore how ideology, faith, memory, and desire shape the places we inhabit. In this program, he will take us on a visual journey through selected works, organized along Kao Chien-Hui’s narrative arc of “Yao’s Black Divine Comedy.” Moving from reimagined shanshui and abandoned infrastructure to contemporary sacred sites, his presentation will reveal landscape as a charged field of power, belief, absurdity, and longing. Yao will be joined by critic, curator, and cultural historian Kao Chien-Hui, who will open the program by situating Yao’s practice—and landscape art more broadly—within Taiwan’s layered histories of migration, colonialism, martial law, and contested boundaries. Following Yao’s presentation, their dialogue will draw on Kao’s conceptual framework for Landscape as Storytelling to consider landscape as a reflexive mirror, a field of resistance, a mode of seeing, an awakening to boundaries, a shift in perception, and a form of situated knowledge. About the Speakers  Yao Jui-Chung Yao Jui-Chung is a Taipei-based artist whose multidisciplinary practice spans painting, photography, installation, video, and documentary research. His work examines Taiwanese identity, ideology, religious belief, historical memory, and the absurdity of the human condition. Major projects include Mirage: Disused Public Property in Taiwan, a long-term collab

939.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 956.summary: Opening Day | \"Ink Shower: Contemporary Taiwanese Artists Reimagine Tradition\" Exhibition
956.description: Opening day for the new exhibition Ink Shower: Contemporary Taiwanese Artists Reimagine Tradition, curated by Kai-Ching Hsiao and Maureen Warren. On view through February 27.  Ink Shower features painting, sculpture, photography, animation, and other digital media that celebrate recent contemporary Taiwanese contributions to the tradition of ink painting. For more than a thousand years, artists have used monochromatic ink to their society’s deepest beliefs and highest aspirations. This tradition continues to provide a compelling means of communicating ideas about spiritual refinement and the relationships between humankind and natural and cosmic forces. The tradition of ink painting also offers a rich visual vocabulary and intellectual framework to reconsider present-day concerns about climate change, consumerism, an increasingly digital world, and more. Audiences interested in the resilience of tradition, the place of humanity vis-a-vis nature and the cosmos in an increasingly technologically complex and globally connected world will enjoy Ink Shower.  Hours: Tue–Fri 10–5 | Sat 10–4 | Thu until 8 pm  Parking nearby is free after 5 pm and on weekends.   This exhibitions was produced in collaboration with the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies at the University of Illinois, with special thanks to Director Matt Winters and Associate Director Yuchia Chang. Ink Shower is organized by InART Space and Krannert Art Museum. Advised by Jamie Tu, Rita Chang, Chien-Hui Kao, Yu-Chia Chang. Made possible with grant support from the Ministry of Culture, Taiwan; Center for Advanced Study MillerComm Lecture Series; and Illinois Arts Council. Additional funding is provided by the J. Fred and Donna Giertz Exhibition Support Fund.
956.location: Krannert Art Museum, 500 E. Peabody Dr., Champaign

957.summary: Food For Thought | Fahad Mahmood and Aleksei Aksimentiev
957.description: Food for Thought: A series of public events featuring research and creative projects by recent CAS Associates and Fellows. We are delighted to showcase the work of some of our most productive and creative faculty in this informal series of intellectually and spiritually invigorating presentations. You are invited to drop in when you can to learn about the exciting projects undertaken by our faculty. 11:00am-11:45am: Fahad Mahmood, CAS Beckman Fellow 2023-24, Physics More information to come!  Noon-12:45pm: Aleksei Aksimentiev, CAS Associate 2025-26, Physics  What we learned from modeling viruses on supercomputers  Viruses sit at the interface of physics and biology: they are compact, compositionally simple assemblies that invite mechanistic modeling, yet they are also major agents of human disease and targets for vaccines and antivirals. Recent advances in supercomputer hardware and the development of multiresolution computational methods have made it possible to simulate complete viral particles using physics-based models. This lecture will share insights gained from these simulations and explore opportunities for further development.
957.location: Levis Faculty Center, Room 208, 919 W Illinois St

962.summary: Exhibition | Ink Shower: Contemporary Taiwanese Artists Reimagine Tradition
962.description: For more than a thousand years, ink painting has been a venerable practice, conveying people’s deepest beliefs and highest aspirations. Ink art has expressed complex, evolving ideas about aesthetics, spirituality, and the nature of the human condition. In today’s world, the range of visual and cultural concerns at the heart of ink art—developed into a major artistic tradition in China during the Tang dynasty (618–907)—now informs a wide range of art, including painting, sculpture, video, photography, animation, and more. Ink Shower focuses on dynamic works of art in this vein produced by twelve Taiwanese artists. While the cultural fabric of Taiwan has been shaped by waves of colonialism, modernization, and globalization, the tradition of ink art in Taiwan has never been a mere continuation of history. Instead, it has evolved through a process of cultural bricolage—appropriating and transforming elements to create new meanings. Rooted in the genealogy of Chinese ink traditions, ink art in Taiwan has been deeply intertwined with local artistic developments since the mid-twentieth century. Over time, the singular path of “ink as tradition” has been gradually dismantled through movements such as modern ink painting, nativist realism, and conceptual art. Taiwanese artists have come to regard ink not merely as a medium, but as a conceptual device and cultural signifier—shifting from medium to spirit, and from spirit to a renewed engagement with diverse media. Ink Shower does not assert a direct narrative. Rather, it adopts an oblique, mobile, and peripheral strategy—entering from the margins, unfolding from dim light, and transforming “ink” into a cultural tool for understanding identity, reimagining history, and envisioning the future. Situating “ink” as a mixture of aesthetic and cultural concerns rather than simply a medium, the exhibition incorporates a range of media to celebrate several distinctively Taiwanese contributions to this enduring and malleable tradition.
962.location: Krannert Art Museum | Main Level | East Gallery

1080.summary: Slavic Department Lecture: \"Whose Tongue Is it Anyway?: On Poets Translating Themselves and Others\"
1080.description: Translators who translate from their “first” language and into their acquired tongue have been marginalized—sometimes despite having won acclaim as original authors in English—but there seems to be a shift in how their work is perceived. Indeed, as more translators begin to engage with the practice, which not only helps to redefine the role of the translator but also our understanding of the literatures of the countries represented, this talk aims to build on the work of Elizabeth Klosty Beaujour, Adrian Wanner, and others in looking at several Polish and Polish-American poets for whom literary multilingualism and translation are two sides of the same coin.  Among Piotr Florczyk’s more than two dozen books of criticism, poetry, essays, and translations are an essay collaboration with Ilya Kaminsky called Within, Without: On Two Cities (Seagull Books, 2026), Dialogue and Influence: Essays on Polish and American Poets (Academic Studies Press, 2025), Polish Literature as World Literature (co-edited with K.A. Wisniewski, Bloomsbury, 2023), and Swimming Pool, an Object Lessons title, which has just been translated into Polish. His honors include the Harold Morton Landon Translation Award from the American Academy of Poets as well as fellowships from the Wisława Szymborska Foundation and the Polish Book Institute. Florczyk is Associate Professor at UW-Seattle, where he teaches global literary studies. For more info about him and his work, please visit: www.piotrflorczyk.com

This week's speaker: Augustus Wood Dr. Augustus Wood is a historian and Assistant Professor at the University of Illinois School of Labor and Employment Relations. He is a scholar of African American History of the Urban South with an interdisciplinary focus on political economy, intra-racial class struggle, working class social movements, and gentrification in modern urban regions. 1132.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 1144.summary: Decoding the Page: Emblems, Ornaments, and Early Modern Reading
1144.description: This event will highlight the collaborative project involving Emblematica (University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign), a digital library of emblem books, and Compositor (University of Birmingham), a database of printers’ ornaments. Dr. Hazel Wilkinson hypothesizes that “emblem-literacy” caused readers to engage with ornamented books in ways previously unaccounted-for in scholarship. This event is open to the public and all audiences are welcome! Refreshments will be served.

1215.description: Chado, or the Way of Tea, is one of the most ancient and revered arts of Japan and is at the very heart of Japan House. It is a ceremonial way of preparing and serving matcha (powdered green tea) that benefits both the host and the guest through mutual respect, non-verbal communication, and a calmness, or sense of peace, away from everyday life.There are many different variations of this revered 500-year-old art form. Traditionally, guests sit in the seiza posture on the tatami mats (kneeling with legs folded underneath and resting on the heels). There is also a variety of tea ceremony in which one sits on a chair while drinking the tea called ryūrei style, or table-style tea ceremony. Historically in Japan, people didn't use chairs. They sat on elevated tatami flooring for most everything, even to eat meals. The ryūrei style of tea ceremony was created by Gengensai Seichū (1810-1877), the 11th head of the Urasenke School of Tea, for an exposition held in 1872 in Kyoto. Many foreigners visited Japan for the first time during this expo, so the government requested that an effort be made to modify the traditional form of tea ceremony as a way of making it more accessible. The main feature of ryūrei style is that both host and guests sit on a chair. The seiza posture is no longer used, but utensils are used in the same way as in a normal tea ceremony. Although this one aspect of the ceremony is altered, the ryūrei style is otherwise the same as a tea ceremony seated on tatami using the seiza posture. Even Japanese people, who use the seiza posture much less than in the past, embrace the ryūrei style of tea ceremony because it places less of a burden on the legs and is more physically accessible. We will be alternating weekly between ryūrei (sitting on chairs) and on tatami mats (sitting cross-legged on the tearoom floor). 1335.description: Nutrition for Cats: Rethinking the Basics  We are pleased to invite you to a free live webinar featuring Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas.  Date: Tuesday, December 1, 2026  Time: 3:00 – 4:00 PM CT Format: Live Online Webinar     Dr. Mariana Fragoso Rentas is a Brazilian veterinarian, professor, researcher, and specialist in companion animal nutrition. She earned her DVM, Master’s, and PhD in Animal Nutrition and Production from the School of Veterinary Medicine and Animal Science of the University of São Paulo (FMVZ-USP), with a strong focus on companion animal nutrition. Her professional experience spans clinical nutrition, small animal medicine, university teaching, scientific research, and technical training in the pet food industry. She currently serves as a university professor in Brazil and is the Director of the Veterinary Teaching Hospital at UNINTA Fortaleza. Cats have unique nutritional requirements that are often misunderstood or oversimplified. In this session, Dr. Rentas will revisit the foundations of feline nutrition, discuss common misconceptions, and examine how modern research is influencing approaches to long-term feline health and wellbeing. Sign up for the mailing list to receive the webinar link and updates.https://go.illinois.edu/ipets-webinars

1367.description: Handel’s Messiah remains one of the most enduring and beloved works in the choral repertoire, offering a profound synthesis of musical beauty and spiritual reflection. From the celebratory brilliance of the “Hallelujah” chorus to the introspective lyricism of its arias, Messiah traverses a wide emotional and theological landscape. Its carefully crafted structure and expressive clarity exemplify Handel’s dramatic genius. This performance invites audiences to engage with a work that continues to inspire through its balance of grandeur, intimacy, and a timeless holiday message. Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: Handel's Messiah

1388.summary: Planetary Architectures and Insights Towards Planet Formation
1388.description: After a brief discussion about the types of exoplanetary architectures discovered so far, I will focus on one sub-population and what we can learn about planet formation by studying it in depth. Hot Jupiters were long thought to be lonely planets. This correctly describes the majority of the population and strongly motivates high-eccentricity tidal migration as the most common method of taking a hot Jupiter to its final short-period orbit. However, a growing number of systems now reveal nearby planetary companions. In this talk, I will discuss recent theoretical and observational results exploring the origin and evolution of hot Jupiters, with a particular focus on those with adjacent companion planets. I show that high-eccentricity tidal migration is generally incompatible with the survival of close-in companions except in very particular scenarios. I further demonstrate that while inner companions are dynamically robust, outer companions can be driven out of the transiting plane through secular interactions, stellar evolution, and stellar obliquity, potentially explaining their apparent absence in some systems. With this in mind, I present the discovery and characterization of the TOI-4468 system as a case study, highlighting how its unique architecture (an outer companion planet, but no inner companion) constrains its dynamical history. The full observational evidence suggests that while most isolated hot Jupiters likely formed through tidal migration, systems with nearby companions preferentially assembled in dynamically cold, disk-mediated ways, revealing multiple formation pathways for close-in giant planets.

1430.description: Get up to speed on using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide to make Canvas pages more accessible for everyone! We’ll discuss the limitations of the tool and what still needs to be checked manually using basic digital accessibility principles. By the end of this workshop, you’ll understand how to fix Canvas pages using the Pope Tech Canvas Accessibility Guide tool and be well on the way to creating inclusive Canvas pages that meet State and Federal accessibility standards.

1488.summary: School Performance: Step Afrika! presents The Fruits of Our Labor (KCYS)
1488.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Celebrate the body as an instrument with Step Afrika!, the GUINNESS WORLD RECORDS™ title holder for the Largest Stepping Dance and the world’s leading authority on the art form of stepping. The company’s newest work, The Fruits of Our Labor, blends the power of body percussion and contemporary dance with the vibrant energy of isipantsula (a rhythmic dance originating in South African townships) and the South African gumboot dance. Long-time Step Afrika! collaborator Jakari Sherman and South African choreographer Vusi Mdoyi lead an ensemble of virtuosic dancers whose bodies become instruments—clapping, striking, and stepping in mesmerizing unison, merging rhythm and ritual, history and storytelling. Recommended for grades 3 and up Learn more about School Performance: Step Afrika! presents The Fruits of Our Labor (KCYS)

1492.summary: The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench
1492.description: The Chicago-based Neo-Futurists have been writing and performing 30 plays in 60 minutes since 1988. Each play offers something different: be it funny, profound, elegant, disgusting, topical, irreverent, terrifying, or a song, all are original and truthful, tackling the here-and-now, and inspired by the lived experiences of the performers. “The ingenuity and engagement of the work not only remains but has deepened . . . the ensemble maps thorny social, psychological, and political terrain with foolishness and ferocity,” says the Chicago Reader. With new plays every week, The Infinite Wrench is The Neo-Futurists’ ongoing and ever-changing attempt to shift the conventions of live performance and speak to those unreached or unmoved by traditional theatre. Learn more about The Neo-Futurists present The Infinite Wrench

1511.description: Krannert Center’s annual visit by the Mark Morris Dance Group features a new, family-friendly dance and music production staged and choreographed by Mark Morris. The joyful, all-ages Holidayland celebrates the richness and diversity of communal traditions across cultures and seasons. The story, written by bestselling Goosebumps author R.L. Stein, finds two siblings encountering a magic village that bursts into light, music, and celebration one day each year, remaining cloaked in darkness the rest of the year. As the celebration fades and shadows return, the siblings emerge transformed, holding fast to the beauty, mystery, and delight of what they witnessed. Morris’s exceptional creative team includes acclaimed composer Nico Muhly, Obie Award-winning scenic designer Allen Moyer, longtime costume collaborator Elizabeth Kurtzman, and lighting designer Mike Faba, with MMDG Music Director Colin Fowler leading the six-piece ensemble that integrates all components of the production. Learn more about Mark Morris Dance Group and Music Ensemble: Holidayland

1517.description: Landscapes in Sound and Ink explores the rich dialogue between Taiwanese visual art and music. Presented in conjunction with the Ink Shower exhibition at the Krannert Art Museum and produced in collaboration with the Center for East Asian and Pacific Studies, this program brings together works inspired by landscape, memory, nature, and cultural identity.  Featuring music by Taiwanese composers for piano trio and solo piano, the concert reflects the poetic atmosphere of ink painting traditions through sound, evoking mountains, water, mist, and shifting emotional landscapes. Through the interplay of visual art and music, audiences are invited to experience how musical textures and colors parallel the expressive brushwork and spatial imagination found in Taiwanese ink paintings. This collaborative event celebrates Taiwan’s artistic heritage while fostering cross-cultural understanding through music and visual art. This event is free to attend. 1524.summary: Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose
1524.description: Join performer and educator, Seth Stewart, as he shares valuable and relatable lessons he’s learned in his journey to a successful career as an actor, dancer, choreographer, and leading performing arts educator. Audience questions will be welcomed during a Q&A session following Stewart’s talk. Stewart was an original cast member of Hamilton and performed in other Broadway shows including Sweet Charity and In the Heights. He has toured the world with popular artists such as Madonna, Jennifer Lopez, Mariah Carey, and more; appeared in movies like Sex and the City: The Movie and Music and Lyrics; as well as choreographed for the television show Bull, the Nickelodeon Kids’ Choice Awards, among others. In 2025, Stewart published his first book, Follow Your Vision, Live Your Truth, a memoir chronicling his journey from Broadway to a decade-long transformational spiritual journey that led him back to nature and his heart. Today, he serves as a performance coach and guest speaker through his company, Performer’s Edge, which provides coaching, courses, and workshops for pre-professional and professional artists – giving them the tools to succeed in the entertainment industry. Stewart is also the founder of True Kings Academy, a mentorship program supporting men with leadership skills through spiritual embodiment, mental health wellness, and wealth mindset. This event is sponsored by the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs. Learn more about Seth Stewart: From Passion to Purpose

1528.description: Acclaimed bassist Edgar Meyer, mandolin virtuoso Mike Marshall, and composer-violinist George Meyer unite as “Meyer, Marshall, Meyer” for an evening of inventive, genre-crossing music. A MacArthur Fellow and multiple Grammy Award winner, Edgar Meyer is widely regarded as one of the leading bassists of his generation, known for his work across classical, bluegrass, and contemporary music. Mike Marshall, a three-time Grammy nominee, has released more than 40 recordings and is celebrated for his fluency across bluegrass, jazz, classical, and Brazilian traditions. George Meyer brings a distinctive compositional voice shaped by both classical and fiddle traditions, with commissions and performances spanning major festivals and venues nationwide. Together, these longtime collaborators revisit and expand the repertoire of Edgar Meyer’s landmark project Short Trip Home, along with new works written for this ensemble, blending their individual and collective talents in an extraordinary program. Learn more about Meyer, Marshall, Meyer

After recent New York appearances, the group embarks on its first US and European tour this spring, showcasing a dynamic, intimate sound shaped by deep interplay and intensity. 1564.summary: Sinfonia da Camera: From Brahms with Love
1564.description: Celebrating Valentine’s weekend, this program centers on the music of Johannes Brahms, whose works embody warmth, lyricism, and profound emotional depth. Alongside his music, Clara Schumann’s Konzertsatz in F Minor offers a compelling opening, reflecting her distinctive voice as both composer and pianist, as well as her close and deeply intimate artistic friendship with Brahms. Brahms’s Hungarian Dances (Nos. 1, 3, and 10) bring vibrant energy and rhythmic vitality, drawing on folk traditions with characteristic refinement. At the heart of the program, the Double Concerto in A Minor, performed by violinist Lucia Lin and cellist Owen Young, unfolds as an intimate musical dialogue of two voices in expressive conversation. The concert concludes with Brahms’s Symphony No. 2 in D Major, a radiant and expansive work whose pastoral beauty offers a luminous and deeply affectionate close. Program: Clara Schumann: Konzertsatz in F Minor for piano and orchestra Ian Hobson, piano and conductor Johannes Brahms: Hungarian Dances Nos. 1, 3, and 10 Johannes Brahms: Double Concerto in A Minor, Op. 102 Lucia Lin, violin; Owen Young, cello Johannes Brahms: Symphony No. 2 in D Major, Op. 73 Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: From Brahms with Love

1572.summary: Seminar Series - Professor Brenda Wilson, Dept. of Microbiology
1572.description: Beyond the Point-of-No-Return - Designer Toxin-Mediated Biothreats Bio: Brenda Anne Wilson, Ph.D., is a professor of microbiology and the Associate Director of Undergraduate Education in the School of Molecular & Cellular Biology at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign (UIUC). She holds joint appointments in pathobiology at the College of Veterinary Medicine and in biomedical and translational sciences at the Carle Illinois College of Medicine. She is the Illinois Faculty Fellow for Sandia National Laboratories in the Office of the Vice Chancellor for Research and Innovation.   After completing her B.A. in biochemistry and German from Barnard College at Columbia University, she was a DAAD graduate fellow of biochemistry at the Ludwig-Maximilians Universität München in Germany, studying virus labeling for in vivo tracking. She then earned her M.A. and Ph.D. degrees in chemistry from the Johns Hopkins University, where she received the Ernest M. Marks Achievement Award and an AAUW doctoral fellowship to study antibiotic biosynthesis. She began her studies on bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins as an NIH-postdoctoral fellow in microbiology at Harvard Medical School, and during her first tenured faculty appointment in biochemistry at Wright State University School of Medicine.   Wilson's current research focuses on the host-microbe interface; bacterial pathogenesis and bacterial protein toxins; development of anti-toxin and toxin-based biologics; and comparative and functional genomic technologies and applications involving microbiomes in health and disease.

1586.summary: Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne
1586.description: It has been more than 30 years since the celebrated violinist Midori graced the stage of the Foellinger Great Hall. Midori, once a child prodigy, is now a violin superstar recognized as a visionary educator and humanitarian whose multiple nonprofit organizations bring music to children and underserved communities. The United Nations appointed Midori a Messenger of Peace in 2007; she was named a Kennedy Center Honoree in 2021. “In her hands,” said Roberto Prosseda when conferring the 2025 Cremona Musica Award, “the violin is not only an instrument—it becomes a voice for humanity itself.” Midori has enjoyed a longstanding partnership with the Festival Strings Lucerne, a brilliant European chamber ensemble under the leadership of Daniel Dodds. This concert features two works by Mendelssohn: his beloved Violin Concerto and the “Scottish” Symphony. The performance also includes works by Maurice Ravel and Helena Winkelman, both of which pay homage to Haydn. Learn more about Midori, violin with Festival Strings Lucerne

1587.description: “Theatre is a doorway,” says illusionist Scott Silven. “A place where we gather in the dark, drawn together by stories that remind us who we are, who we were, and who we might become. It’s where we witness the impossible, feel the weight of the past, and step into the unknown, together. And The Lost Things is about that unknown.” A joyful exploration of wonder, memory, and shared experience, Silven’s awe-inspiring 75-minute show reveals the mysterious side of human nature through breathtaking illusions and an evocative narrative. Directed by Graham McLaren and designed by Jamie Vartan, The Lost Things reminds you that even in loss, there is beauty to be found—and that sometimes, getting lost is the first step toward truly finding yourself. 1615.summary: Routes, Encounters, Destinations in Medieval Asia (ca. 500–1500)
1615.description: This conference, organized by Gian Piero Persiani (EALC) and Adam Newman (Religion), will bring together scholars working across disciplines to explore how movement, exchange, and place-making shaped the medieval Asian world. Throughout history, people, objects, and knowledge have been on the move, crossing borders, merging in unexpected ways, and continually reshaping cultural and political landscapes. Movement, however, is never abstract—it unfolds through and between places both real and imagined: between origins and destinations, in cities and across frontiers, and along seas, rivers, deserts, and pilgrimage routes. Movement and destination thus exist in a dynamic and dialogical relationship, each defining and transforming the other. This conference examines these entwined histories of mobility and emplacement in Medieval South, Central, and East Asia between 500 and 1500 CE. Participants will approach the topic from diverse methodological and theoretical perspectives, exploring how travel, exchange, and encounter produced religious missions and pilgrimages; facilitated the transmission, translation, and localization of texts and ideas; fostered multilingualism and intertextuality; and animated networks of trade and diplomacy. Equally important will be attention to the physical and imagined sites that anchored these processes—urban centers, frontier zones, ports of exchange, sacred landscapes, and celebrated sites of natural beauty.  Proposed themes include:Pilgrimage and sacred geographies: routes, shrines, and travelers.Routes and networks of knowledge: monastic and scholarly communities, texts, and maps.Cityscapes and landscapes: ports, borderlands, and scenic sites.Multilingualism and translation: linguistic crossings and literary exchange.Trade, objects, and material culture: movement of commodities and artistic forms.

1633.description: KODO is an internationally renowned ensemble dedicated to exploring the limitless rhythmic possibilities of traditional Japanese taiko drumming. The name “KODO” evokes both the “heartbeat,” the primal source of rhythm, and “children of the drum,” reflecting the group’s spirit of vitality and curiosity. Since debuting in 1981, KODO has performed over 7,500 times across more than 50 countries, focusing on cultural connection and human unity. Based on Sado Island off the northwest coast of Japan, KODO blends three core elements in performance: reimagined folk traditions, works by leading composers, and original creations shaped by global influences. Their newest production, Luminance, offers a striking view of KODO’s ever-evolving artistry—fusing powerful taiko with refined theatricality, dynamic choreography, and moments of shimmering stillness. The result is an immersive concert experience that pulses with energy, precision, and a radiant sense of shared human rhythm. Learn more about KODO presents LUMINANCE

1644.description: Oscar-nominated filmmaker Sam Green collaborates with National Book Critics Awardee and environmentalist Rebecca Solnit for the latest of his “live cinema” experiences. In Green’s work, documentary film meets live original music with Green’s own live narration. It’s “a singular experience, and a collective one, with the potential for human connection and human errors” notes The New York Times. Trees is a profoundly moving study of humankind’s relationship to our earthly cohabitants, the silent witnesses to all of humanity across countless events and generations, putting humanity’s place into perspective. Directed and performed by Sam Green with cinematography by Yoni Brook, and featuring actress Judi Dench, poet laureate Ada Limón, scientists, and stories from around the world, Trees marks Green’s most ambitious film yet. Trees is produced by ArKtype and Josh Penn and supported in part by the National Endowment for the Arts. Commissioning partners: The Boston Symphony Orchestra; New World Symphony; Oregon Symphony Orchestra; Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts; Wiener Festwochen; Barbican Centre; Holland Festival; Stanford Live @ Stanford University; Duke Arts @ Duke University, Durham, NC; The Arts Center at NYU Abu Dhabi; Green Music Center of Sonoma State University; and Arizona Arts Live at University of Arizona Learn more about Sam Green presents Trees

1650.summary: 2027 Gryphon Lecture: School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas
1650.description: Jonna Perrillo, education historian and professor of English education at the University of Texas at El Paso, will deliver the 2027 Gryphon Lecture hosted by the Center for Children's Books in the School of Information Sciences. She will present \"School Book Lists and the Civic Education of U.S. Teens: from 1950 to Texas.\" Bio: Jonna Perrillo's scholarship focuses on humanities education and social citizenship formation, both historically and in contemporary schools. She is the author of three books: Uncivil Rights: Teachers, Unions, and the Battle for School Equity (winner of the New Scholar Book Award from the American Education Research Association, 2013) and Educating the Enemy: Teaching Nazis and Mexicans in the Cold War Borderlands (winner of the Southwest Book Award from the Border Regional Library Association, 2023, and the Bolton-Cutter Prize from the Western History Association, 2022, and Uncensored: Educators Speak Out on Teaching in the Time of Book Bans (Harvard Education Press, 2026). Her writing and research have been featured in The New York Times, The Washington Post, TIME magazine, the Boston Review, Education Week, Slate, Post45, The 74 and on PBS and National Public Radio. With Dr. Andrew Newman, she is the three-time co-director of the National Endowment for the Humanities Summer Institute for Teachers, “Making the Good Reader and Citizen: The History of Literature Instruction in American Schools.” In June 2026, she and Newman co-published the open access report \"Atomized English: Fewer Whole Books, More Isolated Learning Experiences.\"

1735.summary: Renée Elise Goldsberry with Illinois Wind Symphony
1735.description: The premier wind ensemble of the University of Illinois School of Music and its conductor Kevin M. Geraldi welcome acclaimed singer/actor/songwriter Renée Elise Goldsberry for a high-energy, nondenominational spiritual journey reminiscent of a good old-fashioned revival. The Tony- and Grammy-winning, three-time Emmy Award-nominated Goldsberry is renowned for her performance as Angelica Schuyler in the Broadway phenomenon Hamilton. Her Broadway credits also include starring roles in The Color Purple, The Lion King, and Rent, not to mention a variety of roles across film and television, including Ally McBeal, One Life to Live, She Hulk: Attorney at Law, and the titular role in The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks. Using jazz, blues, pop, rock, soul, folk, and Broadway showtunes, Goldsberry invites you to fall in love with love—brother love, sister love, love of humanity—to remember who we are and what unifies us. Learn more about Renée Elise Goldsberry with Illinois Wind Symphony

1744.summary: Seminar Series - Matt Caplan, Associate Professor, Dept. of Physics, Illinois State University
1744.description: Bio: Dr. Caplan joined ISU in the fall of 2019. His PhD from Indiana University in 2017 won the Dissertation Award in Nuclear Physics from the APS, and prior to joining ISU Dr. Caplan was a CITA National Fellow at the McGill Space Institute.  At ISU, he is the chair of the Twelve Thousand Bombs seminar series on nuclear weapons. Outside academia, he is a writer and scientific consultant for the YouTube channels \"In a Nutshell\" by Kurzgesagt and \"PBS Space Time\" by PBS Digital Studio, with writing credits on nearly 100 videos with combined view counts of a billion.  In 2021, Dr. Caplan was an inaugural Next-Generation Fellow of the Physicists Coalition for Nuclear Threat Reduction. He won a Cottrell Scholar Award in 2023, he is a Kavli Scholar of the Kavli Institute for Theoretical Physics at UCSB (2022-2024), and he is a co-investigator of the Simons Collaboration on Extreme Electrodynamics of Compact Sources (SCEECS).

1755.description: The Chicago Symphony’s trademark power and brilliance will be on full display when the distinguished Swiss conductor Philippe Jordan steps onto the podium to lead Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 4. From the opening brassy fanfare to its gorgeous melodies and emotional intensity, Tchaikovsky’s breakthrough masterpiece swings from dark despair to exuberant triumph. The concert begins with Wagner’s Overture to Rienzi before showcasing Musical America’s Instrumentalist of the Year, violinist Augustin Hadelich, in the cinematic and virtuosic Violin Concerto by Korngold. “The essence of Hadelich’s playing,” wrote Robert Battey in The Washington Post, “is beauty: reveling in the myriad ways of making a phrase come alive on the violin, delivering the musical message with no technical impediments whatsoever, and thereby revealing something from a plane beyond ours.” Learn more about Chicago Symphony Orchestra

1800.summary: Stanley Clarke & Hiromi along with PUBLIQuartet - A Celebration of the Music of Chick Corea
1800.description: National Endowment for the Arts Jazz Master Stanley Clarke joins forces with acclaimed pianist Hiromi—both Grammy Award winners—for a powerful tribute to the late Chick Corea. Blending Corea’s iconic compositions with original works inspired by his legacy, the program celebrates a towering figure whose influence spanned bebop, fusion, and beyond. Clarke, Corea’s longtime collaborator in Return to Forever, and Hiromi—mentored by Corea from a young age—honor a shared musical lineage rooted in innovation and expressive freedom. They are joined by PUBLIQuartet, a Grammy-nominated ensemble praised by The Washington Post and The New Yorker for its bold, genre-defying approach to chamber music. This collaboration offers a dynamic and deeply personal celebration of Corea’s enduring impact on the music of our time. Learn more about Stanley Clarke & Hiromi along with PUBLIQuartet - A Celebration of the Music of Chick Corea

1805.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. Grammy-nominated children’s artist Uncle Jumbo layers heartfelt lyrics with high-energy music and interactive dance-alongs that get audiences moving together, inspiring young people to dream big, care for one another, and celebrate what makes them unique. A Texas-born son of a disco and reggae DJ, Uncle Jumbo got his start at age four, playing accordion with touring Zydeco bands on his Aunt Helen’s Louisiana porch. Known for his uplifting spirit and magnetic stage presence, he began creating music for children after the birth of his daughter. Her diagnosis with a rare liver disease, and surgery at only three weeks old, sparked a profound gratitude for life and a mission to help raise generations of positive, loving people as One Big Family. “Imagine that somewhere in the untapped treasures of the late Prince’s legendary vault of music is an album made for kids . . . That’s what Uncle Jumbo sounds like.” (Houston Press) Recommended for grades Pre K – 2 Learn more about School Performance: Uncle Jumbo (KCYS)

1811.description: “Damn the Man, Save the Empire!” This story of betrayal and corruption comes to life in an interactive/immersive 1990s punk/grunge concert venue. Adapted by Anne Kolaczkowski-Magee and directed by Genesee Spridco, this Shakespeare adaptation pulls back the curtains to the gritty DIY politics of Rome. The audience, as citizens, have a role to play in determining the fate of the country. Will they Damn the Man? Will they Save the Empire? Or will they destroy it? Grab your Doc Martens and favorite band t-shirt and come get swept up in the rhythms of fate and conspiracy! Learn more about Illinois Theatre: Julius Caesar

1812.description: Layli Long Soldier is the author of the collections We (Graywolf, 2026), and Whereas (Graywolf Press, 2017), which won the National Book Critics Circle award, the 2018 PEN/Jean Stein Book Award, and was a finalist for the National Book Award. She also wrote the chapbook Chromosomory (Q Ave Press, 2010), and her work has been widely anthologized in books like Native Voices (Tupelo Press, 2019) and The Larger Voice (NACF, 2022). On Whereas, poet Dean Rader remarks, “What is especially compelling about Long Soldier is that she not only undermines language, she undermines form as well. Elsewhere, I have written about the importance of ‘compositional resistance’ for Native poets. By this, I refer to how a poet composes her poem, the form it takes, how it looks on the page, how its typography expresses itself. Whereas is a masterful example of compositional resistance.” Her poems and critical work have appeared in POETRY Magazine, The New York Times, American Poet, The American Reader, The Kenyon Review, BOMB, American Indian Journal of Culture and Research, PEN America, and The Brooklyn Rail, among many others. In 2015, Long Soldier was awarded a National Artist Fellowship from the Native Arts and Cultures Foundation and a Lannan Literary Fellowship for Poetry. She was awarded a Whiting Writer’s Award in 2016 and was shortlisted for the Griffin Poetry Prize in 2018. In 2021, she received an Academy of Arts and Letters Award for Literature and the Michael Murphy Memorial Poetry Prize in the UK. Long Soldier earned a BFA from the Institute of American Indian Arts and an MFA from Bard College. She teaches in the MFA Creative Writing Program at the Institute of American Indian Arts and serves as the 2024-25 Endowed Chair at Texas State University. She resides in Santa Fe, New Mexico.

1829.description: Sinfonia da Camera concludes its season with a program that explores transformation and renewal through music of extraordinary scope and intensity. David DeBoor Canfield’s Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression opens the concert with a work of solemn reflection and contemporary resonance. Stravinsky’s Firebird follows, illuminating the orchestra with its vivid orchestration and mythic narrative of rebirth. Franz Liszt’s Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, conducted from the piano by Ian Hobson, showcases a bold integration of virtuosity and symphonic structure. The season concludes with Tchaikovsky’s Symphony No. 5, a powerful journey from darkness to affirmation. With its sweeping themes and triumphant conclusion, the symphony offers a fitting culmination to a season defined by expressive depth and artistic ambition. Program: David DeBoor Canfield: Overture: Threnody for the Victims of Military Aggression Igor Stravinsky: The Firebird Franz Liszt: Piano Concerto No. 1 in E-flat Major, S.124 Ian Hobson, piano and conductor Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky: Symphony No. 5 in E Minor, Op. 64 Learn more about Sinfonia da Camera: Firebird Finale

1834.description: The Jupiter String Quartet chose its name because the planet Jupiter was prominent in the night sky at the time of the quartet’s formation in 2001. A particularly intimate group consisting of violinists Mélanie Clapiès and Meg Freivogel, violist Liz Freivogel (Meg’s older sister), and cellist Daniel McDonough (Meg’s husband, Liz’s brother-in-law), the ensemble's star continues to shine brightly as an important voice in the world of chamber music, exuding an energy that is at once friendly, knowledgeable, and adventurous. This program presents Mozart’s String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, “Dissonance” and Beethoven’s String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127, alongside Azerbaijani composer Franghiz Ali-Zadeh’s Oasis (String Quartet No. 4). The evocative 1998 composition captivates with its mixture of sounds and textures, moods and pictures. Program: Mozart: String Quartet No. 19 in C Major, K.465, “Dissonance” Franghiz Ali-Zadeh: “Oasis” (String Quartet No. 4) Beethoven: String Quartet No. 12 in E-flat Major, Op. 127 Learn more about Jupiter String Quartet

1836.summary: School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)
1836.description: This performance is part of the Krannert Center Youth Series, weekday performances for public schools, private schools, and home school groups. It’s the late 1800s, a time of invention. Trains, steamboats, cameras, even electricity are new at the King’s palace in Honolulu. Eleven-year-old Joseph Kekuku accidentally strikes the strings of his guitar with a bolt from a railroad track and unlocks a brand new sound. Hawaiian music—and the music of America—is never the same. Playwright Moses Goods, one of Hawaiʻi’s most prominent theatre artists, in collaboration with Kealakai Center for Pacific Strings, captures the true story of Joseph Kekuku’s invention of the steel guitar (kīkā kila). The multimedia production features a live Hawaiian slide guitar soundtrack and projections as it celebrates innovation, engineering, and the global exchange of ideas and sound. Rich in history, the play also looks forward and encourages children of today to celebrate their voice, culture, and sense of curiosity. Recommended for grades 2-8 Learn more about School Performance: Honolulu Theatre for Youth | Joseph Kekuku and the Voice of the Steel Guitar (KCYS)

1878.description: Created by sweat variant, the acclaimed partnership between artist and MacArthur Fellow Okwui Okpokwasili and director and designer Peter Born, adaku, part 2 continues a speculative trilogy exploring one family’s entanglement with the transatlantic slave trade. Set in a near-future United States, part 2 investigates the embodied consequences of this violent rupture and the erasure of ancestral knowledge. When transmissions lead to sudden remembering, what is unleashed in the imagination of a young woman who's been led to believe she has no history worth remembering? What are the multitude of futures she can now imagine? sweat variant’s multidisciplinary approach invites audiences into cycles of ritual and repair. The presentation of adaku, part 2 by Sweat Variant was made possible by the New England Foundation for the Arts' National Dance Project, with lead funding from the Doris Duke Foundation and the Mellon Foundation. Learn more about sweat variant presents adaku, part 2

1894.description: Experience an unforgettable evening with Audra McDonald. Widely regarded as one of the greatest performers of her generation, McDonald is the only artist to win six Tony Awards across all four acting categories, along with two Grammy Awards, an Emmy, and the National Medal of Arts. In this intimate concert setting, she brings her luminous voice and profound interpretive skill to a richly varied program of Broadway favorites, selections from the Great American Songbook, and more. Backed by her ensemble, McDonald creates a deeply personal connection with audiences, blending technical brilliance with emotional depth and storytelling mastery. Whether on stage or screen, her artistry consistently sets the standard for excellence. This special appearance promises an evening of elegance, warmth, and musical brilliance from a truly iconic performer. Learn more about An Evening with Audra McDonald

2042.summary: Body Talk: Rethinking Body Image & Beauty Standards
2042.description: In our media-focused society, our bodies often feel on display, and we may find ourselves judging our physical appearance or even engaging in behaviors to alter how we look. The Body Talk: Rethinking Body Image & Beauty Standards workshop tries to interrupt the negative thoughts people often have.  This workshop is a body acceptance-based program designed to help students feel better about their bodies as we directly discuss the impact of diversity within cultural appearance ideals (including race, gender identity, sexuality, ability, and age) and critique the individual and collective impact of pursuing exclusive appearance norms. This research-based program has been shown to improve body satisfaction and acceptance among college students and reduce the risks of unhealthy eating behaviors, disordered eating, and eating disorders. The program entails two 90-minute sessions, scheduled one week apart, and is co-led by Counseling Center staff members, graduate assistants, and Counseling Center Paraprofessional undergraduate students. Each session is designed for groups of 6-12 students. To get the most out of the program, individual students and groups are asked to register only if they can attend both 90-minute sessions. Body Talk is targeted toward all shapes and sizes. Students can benefit regardless of gender identity, ethnicity, size, or ability. All registered students are welcome and encouraged to participate!

2048.description: The campus is currently looking for exciting juniors* to nominate for the prestigious Harry S. Truman Scholarship.Are you bothered by an issue and trying to make changes to address a problem?  The Truman program is looking for the academically strong student who has a passion for public service. Evaluators look for leadership ability, potential for influencing public policies, community service and extracurricular involvement, strong academic performance, and potential to perform well in a graduate school program. It awards $30,000 merit-based scholarships to U.S. citizen college students who wish to attend graduate school in preparation for careers in public service.  Public service includes a wide array of career possibilities, such as public health; local, state, or federal government; educational policy; international relations; conservation; and environmental protection. Candidates should be able to demonstrate leadership experiences in campus and community service activities. Truman Scholars have pursued many fields of study, such as agriculture, engineering, economics, education, government, history, international relations, law, political science, public administration, and public health. Scholars are required to work in public service for three of the seven years following completion of a Foundation funded graduate degree program as a condition of receiving funding.  The University of Illinois may nominate up to four students for the Truman Scholarship.  If you are interested in applying, please plan to attend our informational session and discussion with a former Truman Scholar on September 24th from 3:30pm - 4:30pm. We will host an Online Truman Information Session on Sept 25th from 9am - 10am for those unable to attend in-person and a Truman Workshop Session will be held on September 25th from 3:00pm - 4:00pm to help students begin to craft a Truman Application online.  Both sessions will be held in 514 IUB. For more information, contact the scholarships

2107.description: Many students find taking tests, completing assignments, and/or giving presentations very stressful. At times, this stress can be counterproductive and negatively impact performance. The American Test Anxieties Association estimates that between 16 and 20% of college students have high anxiety when it comes to taking tests or performing well on assignments. Fortunately, there are ways to address anxiety so that you can do your best work. During the academic year, we offer drop-in Test Anxiety Workshops. These workshops are free for students, but space is limited, so we request that you register in advance on our website.

2115.description: The Critical Language Scholarship, from the U.S. Department of State, is a fully-funded, intensive overseas language and cultural immersion program for American undergraduate and graduate students.  The CLS institutes cover one academic year of university-level language coursework in 8 to 10 weeks over the summer, and include cultural programming, local language partners, and excursions.  Participants receive academic credit at their U.S. institutions.  Applicants must be U.S. citizens at least 18 years of age and enrolled in a degree-granting program at the undergraduate or graduate level. For more information, please visit: Homepage - Critical Language Scholarship Program Our advisors, will provide an overview of the program and give you helpful guidance on how to put together a competitive application.

2128.description: The University of Illinois will be hosting informational sessions on National Security Education Program Boren undergraduate study abroad scholarships.  Participants will receive information about the program and converse with an Illinois alumni recipient.  The campus application deadline is in January 2027 for any semester or year of study between June 2027 and March 2028. Students are encouraged to begin application drafts prior to leaving for winter break.  The Boren provides study abroad scholarships of up to $25,000 for a full academic year or $12,500 for a semester. Science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) students also have the option of applying for summer-only programs of eight weeks or more. All scholarships may be used for U.S. citizens to study in Asia, Africa, Central & Eastern Europe, Latin America, or the Middle East on almost any study abroad program. These are merit-based scholarships (approximately 1 in 5 eligible applicants receive awards). In order to receive the scholarship, award winners must enter into a service agreement requiring that they attempt to work in a paid position for the federal government in an area related to national security—generally the Departments of State, Defense, Homeland Security, or the Intelligence Community within three years of graduation (deferrals possible/encouraged for graduate study). Working for USAID or tenure in the Peace Corps counts in the service requirement. Winners also receive priority-hiring status.  The Boren information session will be held on October 22, 2026 from 3:30pm - 4:30pm and the Boren workshop will be held on October 23 from 3:00pm - 4:00pm. Both sessions will be held in room 514 IUB. For more information, contact the scholarships office at topscholars@illinois.edu or visit our website at Boren Scholarship – National & International Scholarships Program
2128.location: Illini Union Bookstore Building, fifth floor #514, 807 S Wright St Champaign IL, 61820

2150.summary: Body Talk: Rethinking Body Image & Beauty Standards
2150.description: In our media-focused society, our bodies often feel on display, and we may find ourselves judging our physical appearance or even engaging in behaviors to alter how we look. The Body Talk: Rethinking Body Image & Beauty Standards workshop tries to interrupt the negative thoughts people often have.  This workshop is a body acceptance-based program designed to help students feel better about their bodies as we directly discuss the impact of diversity within cultural appearance ideals (including race, gender identity, sexuality, ability, and age) and critique the individual and collective impact of pursuing exclusive appearance norms. This research-based program has been shown to improve body satisfaction and acceptance among college students and reduce the risks of unhealthy eating behaviors, disordered eating, and eating disorders. The program entails two 90-minute sessions, scheduled one week apart, and is co-led by Counseling Center staff members, graduate assistants, and Counseling Center Paraprofessional undergraduate students. Each session is designed for groups of 6-12 students. To get the most out of the program, individual students and groups are asked to register only if they can attend both 90-minute sessions. Body Talk is targeted toward all shapes and sizes. Students can benefit regardless of gender identity, ethnicity, size, or ability. All registered students are welcome and encouraged to participate!

This two-part program helps students realize when perfectionism is more harmful than good and develop more realistic expectations.    This program is open to all Illinois students—you do not need to be a current client of the Counseling Center to register.

2180.summary: Innovative Teaching to Excel and Advance MedEd (iTEAM)
2180.description: iTEAM is an innovative partnership with the ACGME and is guided by the ACGME Medical Educator Competencies. This academic year program explores essential components for effective teaching in medical education. Nationally recognized presenters, education specialist faculty, and instructional coaches facilitate the experience through a collaborative small-group cohort model. The program blends monthly half-day workshops with asynchronous learning and individualized coaching support. Participants receive observation, feedback, and mentoring to strengthen teaching effectiveness across clinical and educational settings. The series is approved for ACCME continuing education credit. Registration opens each Spring/Summer for the following academic year.

2268.description: Conference Overview AI is rapidly reshaping society, science, and computing. Yet the energy and computational demands of frontier AI is exposing limits on efficiency, sustainability, and accessibility. Realizing AI’s full potential will require more than increasingly capable models; it will require radically new approaches to how AI systems are designed, built, and deployed. This inaugural workshop, Convergent Intelligence: AI hardware Co-design and the Future of Computing, is jointly organized by Pathways to Enable Open Source Ecosystems HLS4ML Project, the Discovery Partners Institute, and the Accelerated AI Algorithms for Data-Driven Discovery Institute, to bring together researchers, engineers, developers, and industry partners to explore new directions to define the future of AI computing. The theme of convergent intelligence is an emerging paradigm for advancing AI in which algorithms, platforms, architectures, design tools, and data resources are co-developed in close coordination to drive innovation. Participants will explore how this integrated approach can advance the frontier of AI & quantum and accelerate discovery.
2268.location: Discovery Partners Institute, 200 South Wacker Drive,  4th Floor Discovery Room, Chicago, IL  60606

2271.description: Plot Twist: Independent Living Skills ARE Employment Skills Independent living skills are often viewed as a separate component of transition planning, yet research shows they play a critical role in employment and postsecondary success. Also referred to as adaptive or life skills, they encompass the knowledge and behaviors needed to navigate home, work, and community life. Skills such as community participation, executive functioning, self-advocacy, transportation, financial literacy, and personal care are essential for obtaining, maintaining, and advancing in employment. In this interactive workshop, participants will learn about the connection between independent living skills and career readiness, examine how these skills impact employment outcomes, and learn practical strategies for embedding them into transition programming. Participants will leave with evidence-based instructional practices, implementation tools, and actionable strategies for teaching essential independent living skills that better prepare students with disabilities for success in work, education, and adult life.

2275.summary: Data Centers as Systems: An Introduction
2275.description: Energy-Water-Compute Nexus Seminar SeriesData Centers as Systems: An IntroductionThursday, October 1, 2026 12:00–1:30 p.m. Discovery Partners Institute (DPI) 200 S. Wacker Drive, 20th Floor, Chicago, IL Rm: CR 2005 Hybrid — In person + virtual Session Description | Responsible AI depends on a full ecosystem — from computing hardware and data centers to cooling systems, energy, water and the materials that make it all possible. This session introduces data centers as systems, bringing together perspectives from higher education, advanced computing and industry to examine the infrastructure behind increasingly intensive AI workloads. The conversation will explore how these systems connect — and help surface the research questions that emerge at their intersection.Featured Speakers Raymond ParpartDirector of Physical Infrastructure & Data Centers University of Chicago & UChicago Medicine Tim BurnerAssociate Director, Integrated Cyberinfrastructure National Center for Supercomputing Applications (NCSA), UIUC Bill SchaumannPrincipal Engineer & Data Center Infrastructure Specialist Burns & McDonnellAbout the SeriesThe systems behind responsible AI.Responsible AI extends across the full ecosystem: hardware, cooling and HVAC, new materials for heat transport, real-time GPU elasticity and the complex trade-offs between energy, water and compute. 2277.description: Plot Twist: Independent Living Skills ARE Employment SkillsIndependent living skills are often viewed as a separate component of transition planning, yet research shows they play a critical role in employment and postsecondary success. Also referred to as adaptive or life skills, they encompass the knowledge and behaviors needed to navigate home, work, and community life. Skills such as community participation, executive functioning, self-advocacy, transportation, financial literacy, and personal care are essential for obtaining, maintaining, and advancing in employment. In this interactive workshop, participants will learn about the connection between independent living skills and career readiness, examine how these skills impact employment outcomes, and learn practical strategies for embedding them into transition programming. Participants will leave with evidence-based instructional practices, implementation tools, and actionable strategies for teaching essential independent living skills that better prepare students with disabilities for success in work, education, and adult life.
